Abstract of Praxis
An Artificial Intelligence–Based Classification and Ranking System for Border Gateway Protocol Incidents in Enterprise Networks

Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) incidents can cause significant service disruption, traffic misrouting, and loss of network reachability in enterprise and Internet-connected environments. Although network monitoring platforms can identify routing changes and generate alerts, determining the type and likely cause of a BGP incident often requires network engineers to manually correlate BGP UPDATE messages, routing state, logs, and other operational telemetry. Distinguishing among prefix hijacks, route leaks, and routing outages can be particularly challenging because these incidents may exhibit overlapping control-plane behaviors. This Praxis develops and evaluates an artificial intelligence–based system for classifying BGP incidents and ranking the most probable incident types to support network troubleshooting and incident analysis.

The study uses historical BGP routing data associated with labeled hijack, route-leak, and outage incidents. BGP UPDATE data are processed into non-overlapping five-minute analytical windows from which 44 behavioral features are extracted. These features characterize announcement and withdrawal activity, prefix dynamics, peer visibility, AS-path structure and instability, origin changes, multi-origin behavior, and AS-path prepending. The behavioral representation is enriched with 14 historical Autonomous System relationship features derived from the Center for Applied Internet Data Analysis (CAIDA) and 16 Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) and Route Origin Validation (ROV) features derived from historical Route Origin Authorization information. The resulting V4 representation contains 74 features per analytical window and incorporates behavioral routing activity, AS-topology context, and route-origin authorization evidence.

The experimental design treats each BGP incident as an independent experimental unit while five-minute windows serve as lower-level machine-learning observations. A development corpus of 993 TRAIN incidents, evenly distributed across 331 hijacks, 331 route leaks, and 331 outages, was used for feature evaluation, model development, grouped cross-validation, feature ablation, imbalance analysis, algorithm comparison, and hyperparameter optimization. Experiments compared behavioral-only and enriched feature variants, Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers, incident-aware weighting strategies, feature-family contributions, and alternative classification architectures. RPKI/ROV information provided particularly useful discriminatory information for hijack classification, while AS-relationship and routing-behavior features contributed to distinguishing route leaks and outages. The final system uses a leakage-safe hierarchical stacking architecture. At the first level, XGBoost models classify five-minute V4 feature vectors and generate probabilities for Hijack, Leak, and Outage. These probabilities are subsequently summarized at the incident level using distributional, confidence, disagreement, and temporal features that characterize how routing evidence evolves across an incident. A second XGBoost classifier uses this incident-level representation to generate final class probabilities and rank the three candidate incident types. Nested cross-validation, multi-seed stability analysis, label-permutation testing, and first- and second-level leakage audits were used to verify the integrity of the stacked architecture before final evaluation.

The frozen final model was evaluated once on a previously sealed Holdout set of 213 incidents containing 71 hijacks, 71 route leaks, and 71 outages. It achieved an incident-level Macro F1 score of 0.9202 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.8801–0.9544, Top-1 accuracy of 0.9202, Top-2 accuracy of 0.9906, and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of 0.9585. Class-specific F1 scores were 0.8777 for Hijack, 0.9041 for Leak, and 0.9787 for Outage. The correct incident type was ranked first for 196 of 213 incidents and within the top two for 211 of 213 incidents. These results demonstrate that combining BGP behavioral features with AS-relationship and route-origin validation information, followed by incident-level temporal aggregation, can provide accurate classification and highly effective ranking of BGP incident types. Chapter 1—Introduction
Background

Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is one of the dynamic routing protocols which learns routes automatically from neighboring routers and updates networks. What makes BGP different from the other dynamic routing protocol is, it is the only routing protocol in the global public internet. Therefore, BGP carries internet wide routing information between Autonomous Systems. What BGP does is it updates routes when traffic, failures or topology changes occur. There are normal updates of routes that is communicated or passed to the neighbor routers and based on the characteristics of how BGP updates happen the update can be a normal update or anomaly. And these anomalies can be categorized into different BGP incidents.

Modern enterprise networks rely heavily on the global Internet’s interdomain routing infrastructure to maintain availability, performance, and resilience of their services. Enterprise networks advertise their network prefixes to the public global network via BGP, and the core infrastructure of the global network is also used BGP as the def facto standard routing protocol to route the prefixes of the enterprise networks for exchanging reachability information between Autonomous Systems. BGP is designed under the assumptions of trust and cooperation among network operators and Internet Service Providers making it inherently vulnerable to configuration errors, routing policy violations and malicious attacks.

Over the past two decades, BGP-related incidents, including route leaks, prefix hijacks, session instabilities, and misconfigurations, have caused large-scale outages affecting critical services across industries. Notable incidents have demonstrated that even short-lived routing anomalies can disrupt enterprise operations, cloud services, and financial markets. As enterprise networks increasingly depend on multiple Internet Service Providers (ISPs), cloud interconnections, and hybrid architectures, the instability and BGP anomalies affecting those infrastructure affects the stability of the enterprise network.

Network Operations Centers often rely on threshold-based alerts, predefined rules, and manual review of BGP updates to identify routing incidents. While these methods can detect that an abnormal condition exists, they often provide limited help in determining the specific cause of the anomaly. As BGP data continues to grow in volume, speed, and complexity, especially from global collectors such as RouteViews and RIPE RIS, traditional rule-based approaches may not provide enough context for timely and accurate troubleshooting. An AI- or machine-learning-based root-cause analysis approach can improve this process by learning patterns from historical BGP incidents and distinguishing among anomaly types such as hijacks, route leaks, and outages. By identifying and ranking the most likely root causes, the model can help network engineers focus their investigation more quickly and take appropriate corrective action once the probable cause is known.
Research Motivation

Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is fundamental to Internet and enterprise routing, yet diagnosing BGP incidents remains a difficult operational task. Modern network-management and monitoring platforms can detect routing changes, neighbor-state transitions, prefix reachability changes, and abnormal control-plane activity; however, these systems often provide alerts and telemetry rather than a clear interpretation of what type of routing incident is occurring. As a result, network engineers are frequently required to examine BGP UPDATE messages, routing tables, AS-path changes, prefix behavior, peer visibility, security-validation information, and other operational evidence to determine what the routing behavior represents.

This challenge is amplified because different BGP incidents can produce overlapping observable symptoms. Prefix hijacks, route leaks, and routing outages may each involve changes in announcements, withdrawals, AS paths, origin Autonomous Systems, prefix visibility, and routing stability. A single routing symptom therefore may not be sufficient to distinguish one incident type from another. The operational problem is not simply detecting that the routing environment has changed, but interpreting multiple control-plane signals together in a way that supports incident diagnosis and prioritization.

The motivation for this Praxis arises from the gap between the large volume of routing telemetry available to network operators and the limited ability of conventional monitoring systems to transform that telemetry into actionable incident-level intelligence. Existing BGP anomaly research has demonstrated methods for detecting abnormal routing behavior, while operational monitoring platforms provide extensive visibility into network state. However, there remains an opportunity to investigate whether machine-learning techniques can combine heterogeneous BGP signals to classify observed incidents and rank the most plausible incident types for further investigation.

This study therefore examines an AI-based approach that integrates behavioral information extracted from BGP UPDATE messages with Autonomous System relationship information and route-origin validation evidence. Rather than relying on a single routing indicator, the proposed approach evaluates multiple dimensions of BGP behavior and produces a ranked assessment of whether an observed incident is most consistent with a Hijack, Leak, or Outage.

The broader motivation is to provide enterprise network operators with a more structured and evidence-driven method for interpreting BGP incidents. By converting large volumes of routing observations into incident-level classifications and ranked hypotheses, the research seeks to improve the usefulness of BGP telemetry during troubleshooting and to support more informed operational decision-making. The work does not replace the network engineer or claim to determine every underlying physical or configuration-level cause; instead, it provides an AI-assisted mechanism for narrowing the incident space and prioritizing the most likely routing explanations.
Problem Statement

Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) incidents can disrupt routing stability, alter network reachability, misdirect traffic, and affect the availability of enterprise services. For mid-size and large organizations, the operational and financial consequences of prolonged network disruption can be substantial. ITIC's 2024 Hourly Cost of Downtime Survey reported that more than 90% of surveyed mid-size and large enterprises indicated that one hour of downtime exceeds $300,000 in associated costs (ITIC, 2024). These potential consequences make effective identification and diagnosis of routing incidents an important component of enterprise network operations.

Although contemporary network-monitoring and routing-analysis platforms provide visibility into BGP neighbor state, route advertisements, withdrawals, prefix reachability, and other control-plane changes, detecting a routing change does not necessarily explain what type of BGP incident the observed behavior represents. Prefix hijacks, route leaks, and routing outages can exhibit overlapping characteristics in BGP UPDATE data, including changes in route origins, AS paths, announcements, withdrawals, prefix visibility, and routing stability. Consequently, individual indicators may be insufficient to reliably distinguish among incident types.

In enterprise operations, network engineers may therefore need to correlate BGP UPDATE messages, routing tables, logs, AS-path information, route-origin authorization status, routing-policy relationships, and other telemetry to interpret an incident. This process can be labor-intensive and dependent on operator expertise, particularly when large volumes of routing updates are generated or when multiple indicators provide conflicting evidence. Traditional monitoring systems can alert operators that routing behavior has changed, but they do not necessarily transform the available control-plane information into an incident-level classification and ranked set of probable routing explanations.

The problem addressed in this Praxis is therefore the lack of a systematic, data-driven approach for combining multiple dimensions of BGP control-plane evidence to classify and rank routing incident types in a form that supports enterprise network investigation. Specifically, the research examines whether behavioral features derived from BGP UPDATE messages, Autonomous System relationship information, and RPKI/ROV route-origin validation evidence can be integrated using machine learning to distinguish among BGP Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents and rank these alternatives according to their predicted probabilities.

Addressing this problem would provide network operators with an evidence-based mechanism for narrowing the incident space and prioritizing investigative hypotheses. The proposed approach is not intended to determine every underlying physical, configuration, or organizational root cause of a routing failure; rather, it seeks to convert complex BGP control-plane observations into actionable classification and ranking information that can assist engineers during incident analysis.
Thesis Statement

An AI-based classification and ranking system that integrates BGP behavioral characteristics, Autonomous System relationship information, and RPKI/ROV route-origin validation can distinguish among BGP hijacks, route leaks, and routing outages and provide probability-based rankings of incident types to support enterprise network incident analysis.

This Praxis demonstrates that heterogeneous BGP control-plane information can be integrated through machine learning to support incident-level classification and ranking. The developed approach transforms BGP UPDATE observations into non-overlapping five-minute analytical windows represented by 44 behavioral features, including announcement and withdrawal activity, prefix dynamics, peer visibility, AS-path characteristics, origin changes, and routing instability. These behavioral features are enriched with 14 CAIDA AS-relationship features and 16 RPKI/ROV features, producing a final 74-feature representation that combines routing behavior, AS-topology context, and route-origin authorization evidence.

The final architecture uses a hierarchical stacking approach in which a first-level XGBoost model generates window-level probabilities for Hijack, Leak, and Outage. These predictions are subsequently aggregated into incident-level features that characterize probability distributions, prediction confidence, disagreement among windows, and the temporal evolution of routing evidence. A second XGBoost classifier then produces the final incident classification and probability-based ranking of the three candidate incident types.

Experimental development was conducted using 993 TRAIN incidents, equally distributed among 331 hijacks, 331 route leaks, and 331 outages. Feature-variant and feature-family ablation experiments demonstrated that different sources of routing information contribute differently to incident discrimination. RPKI/ROV features provided particularly useful information for distinguishing hijacks, while AS-relationship, peer-visibility, and behavioral routing characteristics contributed to differentiating route leaks and outages. Incident-level temporal stacking produced a substantial improvement over simple averaging of window-level probabilities and remained stable under nested cross-validation, multi-seed evaluation, leakage audits, and label-permutation testing.

The frozen final system was evaluated once on a previously sealed Holdout set of 213 incidents, containing 71 incidents from each class. It achieved an incident-level Macro F1 score of 0.9202, Top-1 accuracy of 0.9202, Top-2 accuracy of 0.9906, and Mean Reciprocal Rank of 0.9585. The correct incident type was ranked within the top two candidates for 211 of 213 Holdout incidents. These findings support the thesis that combining heterogeneous BGP routing evidence with incident-level machine-learning aggregation can provide accurate classification and effective ranking of BGP incident types for enterprise network investigation.
Research Objectives

The primary objective of this research is to develop and evaluate an artificial intelligence–based framework for classifying and ranking BGP incidents using control-plane routing behavior and complementary routing-context information. To accomplish this objective, the study seeks to:

Develop a reproducible BGP incident-analysis pipeline that transforms historical BGP UPDATE data associated with documented routing incidents into structured, non-overlapping analytical windows suitable for machine-learning analysis.

Engineer and evaluate BGP behavioral features that characterize routing activity, including announcements and withdrawals, prefix dynamics, peer visibility, AS-path characteristics and instability, origin changes, and AS-path prepending.

Integrate complementary routing-context information by incorporating CAIDA Autonomous System relationship features and historical RPKI/ROV route-origin validation features with BGP behavioral information.

Evaluate the contribution of different feature groups and feature combinations through controlled feature-variant and feature-family ablation experiments to determine which routing signals contribute most to distinguishing BGP hijacks, route leaks, and routing outages.

Develop and compare machine-learning approaches for BGP incident classification and ranking, including Random Forest and XGBoost models, and evaluate whether incident-level temporal aggregation of lower-level BGP observations improves classification and ranking performance.
Address unequal observational representation among incidents by evaluating incident-aware training strategies while preserving each BGP incident as the independent experimental unit.

Establish a leakage-safe and reproducible evaluation methodology using incident-level grouped cross-validation, nested model evaluation, independent data partitions, model-stability analysis, and a previously sealed Final Holdout set.

Evaluate the final system using both classification and ranking metrics, including Macro F1, Top-1 accuracy, Top-2 accuracy, Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR), and class-specific precision, recall, and F1 scores.

Assess the operational applicability and limitations of the proposed approach, including computational classification latency, the distinction between model inference latency and observation time, and the system's potential role in supporting enterprise network incident investigation.
Research Questions and Hypotheses
RQ1: To what extent can machine-learning models accurately classify and rank BGP incidents as Hijack, Leak, or Outage using BGP control-plane data?

RQ2: How do behavioral BGP features, CAIDA Autonomous System relationship features, and RPKI/ROV route-origin validation features contribute to the classification and ranking of different BGP incident types?

RQ3: Does incident-level aggregation of window-level BGP evidence, including probability, confidence, disagreement, and temporal characteristics, improve BGP incident classification and ranking compared with classification based on simple aggregation of window-level predictions?

H1: Machine-learning models trained on BGP control-plane features can distinguish among Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents and rank the correct incident type with measurable classification and ranking performance.

H2: The combination of behavioral, AS-relationship, and RPKI/ROV features provides greater discriminatory information for BGP incident classification than behavioral features alone, with different feature families contributing differently across Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents.

H3: A machine-learning architecture that incorporates incident-level aggregation of window-level BGP evidence will achieve better incident-level classification and ranking performance than a model that relies on simple mean aggregation of window-level class probabilities.
Scope of Research

This research focuses on the analysis, classification, and ranking of Border Gateway Protocol incidents relevant to enterprise networks and their external routing connectivity. The study examines documented BGP incidents using historical control-plane data and evaluates whether machine-learning methods can distinguish among three incident classes: prefix Hijack, route Leak, and routing Outage. The scope of the research includes:
Analysis of BGP UPDATE messages and derived routing behavior, including announcements, withdrawals, prefix dynamics, AS-path characteristics, origin changes, peer visibility, and routing instability.
Use of historical BGP routing data obtained primarily from the University of Oregon RouteViews project and associated documented real-world routing incidents.
Enrichment of BGP behavioral features with Autonomous System relationship information from CAIDA and historical RPKI/ROV route-origin validation information.
Construction and evaluation of machine-learning models using non-overlapping five-minute analytical windows, with BGP incidents treated as the independent experimental unit.
Comparison of feature variants, imbalance-treatment strategies, Random Forest and XGBoost models, and incident-level temporal aggregation approaches.

Evaluation of the final model using both classification and ranking metrics, including Macro F1, Top-1 accuracy, Top-2 accuracy, Mean Reciprocal Rank, and class-specific precision, recall, and F1 scores.
Assessment of computational inference characteristics and the operational applicability of the proposed approach after the required incident observation data and features are available.

The research does not attempt to redesign or modify the BGP protocol, automatically mitigate routing incidents, or determine every underlying physical or configuration-level cause of a routing failure. It also does not claim to provide a fully validated real-time anomaly-detection capability. Experimental Normal-versus-Incident detection was investigated separately, but it remained an auxiliary component rather than part of the final primary classification architecture.

The final system is therefore scoped as a post-window incident classification and ranking framework that assists with interpreting observed BGP incidents rather than as a complete end-to-end detection, mitigation, or remediation platform.
Research Limitations
This study is subject to several limitations:

Data visibility and labeling: The research relies on publicly documented BGP incidents and RouteViews data, which may not capture all enterprise-specific routing policies, private peering relationships, or control-plane activity.
Incident-class scope: The final model classifies and ranks three BGP incident types, Hijack, Leak, and Outage, and does not represent every possible routing anomaly or underlying network failure.

Normal-versus-Incident detection: Experimental detection of Normal versus Incident behavior did not achieve sufficient reliability and was not included as a mandatory component of the final classification architecture. The final system therefore assumes that a BGP incident has already been identified for analysis.

Operational deployment: The model uses five-minute analytical windows and was evaluated as a post-window classification and ranking system. Although the downstream computational process is fast once features are available, complete real-time latency from live BGP UPDATE ingestion through classification was not evaluated and remains an area for future research.

Chapter 2—Literature Review
Introduction

The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is the principal interdomain routing protocol through which Autonomous Systems (ASes) exchange reachability information and implement routing policy across the global Internet. Its path-vector design allows independently administered networks to select and propagate routes according to local economic, engineering, and security objectives rather than according to a single global optimization criterion (Rekhter et al., 2006; Gao, 2001). This flexibility has enabled BGP to support the growth and decentralized administration of the Internet, but it has also preserved important security and operational limitations. Historically, BGP did not provide cryptographic assurance that an announcing AS was authorized to originate a prefix or that an advertised AS path represented an authorized propagation sequence. Consequently, routing instability, configuration errors, route leaks, prefix hijacks, and outages continue to present operational and security risks.

The literature on BGP has developed along several complementary lines. Foundational studies characterize protocol operation, convergence, routing policy, and the measurement of global control-plane behavior. A second body of work examines routing incidents and outages and demonstrates how local configuration errors, unauthorized advertisements, and policy violations can propagate beyond the networks in which they originate. A third line of research focuses on routing-security mechanisms, particularly the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI), Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs), Route Origin Validation (ROV), and BGPsec. A fourth examines AS-level business relationships and the valley-free routing model, which provide contextual information about whether an observed propagation path is consistent with expected customer-provider and peer-to-peer routing policies (Gao, 2001; Luckie et al., 2013; Giotsas et al., 2014).

These security and policy perspectives are particularly relevant when interpreting BGP incidents. An observed origin change, for example, becomes more informative when considered together with whether the prefix-origin pair is authorized by an available ROA. Similarly, an unusual AS path can be evaluated in the context of inferred relationships among adjacent ASes and whether the path is consistent with expected valley-free propagation. RPKI/ROV and AS-relationship information therefore provide complementary context to behavioral observations derived directly from BGP UPDATE messages. This is important because different routing incidents may exhibit overlapping control-plane characteristics, including bursts of UPDATE activity, withdrawals, origin changes, path changes, and changes in routing visibility (Bagnulo et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2025; Rodday et al., 2024).

Machine-learning research has increasingly sought to exploit these observable characteristics. Prior studies have applied support vector machines, hidden Markov models, decision trees, Random Forests, gradient-boosted models, clustering techniques, recurrent neural networks, and graph-based representations to BGP anomaly detection and classification (Al-Rousan & Trajković, 2012; Sanchez et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2021; Romo-Chavero et al., 2025). More recent work has explored semantics-aware analysis, topology-aware representations, and incident localization rather than relying exclusively on threshold-based detection (Chen et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2025; Latif-Martínez et al., 2025). Explainable artificial intelligence techniques have also been investigated as a means of relating model predictions to routing characteristics that network operators can examine and interpret (Kyryk et al., 2025).

Despite this progress, important gaps remain between BGP anomaly research and operational incident analysis. Routing-security mechanisms generally validate specific properties of a route, while anomaly-detection approaches frequently focus on identifying deviations from normal routing behavior. Other approaches specialize in individual incident categories, such as route leaks or prefix hijacks. Comparatively less attention has been given to integrating behavioral routing characteristics, AS-relationship context, and route-origin validation evidence within a common machine-learning framework that distinguishes among multiple plausible BGP incident types and ranks those alternatives at the incident level. This distinction is operationally relevant because detecting a routing change or anomaly does not by itself provide an operator with a structured assessment of whether the observed incident is most consistent with a hijack, route leak, or routing outage.

This chapter reviews the literature supporting the development of an artificial intelligence–based classification and ranking system for BGP incidents in enterprise networks. Section 2.2 reviews foundational BGP operation and measurement. Section 2.3 examines routing incidents and outages. Section 2.4 evaluates BGP security mechanisms, with particular emphasis on RPKI, ROA, ROV, and BGPsec. Section 2.5 reviews AS relationships, routing policies, valley-free routing, and AS-relationship inference. Section 2.6 synthesizes BGP anomaly-detection and classification techniques. Section 2.7 examines machine-learning approaches relevant to network fault detection, classification, and diagnosis. Sections 2.8 and 2.9 identify the research gaps and synthesize the literature that informs the feature representation, model families, and experimental design evaluated in this Praxis.
Foundational Studies on BGP Operation and Measurement

BGP emerged as the Internet evolved from a comparatively simple hierarchy into a federation of independently operated networks. RFC 4271 defines BGP-4 as a path-vector protocol in which routes are associated with path attributes and exchanged over long-lived TCP sessions (Rekhter et al., 2006). Unlike an interior gateway protocol that attempts to optimize a common metric within one administrative domain, BGP allows each AS to express local policy. The resulting route is therefore not necessarily the shortest topological path; it is the path that survives import policy, local preference, path selection, and export policy across a chain of independently controlled networks.

BGP UPDATE messages provide the principal observational unit for many routing studies. An UPDATE can announce Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI), withdraw previously advertised reachability, and carry path attributes such as AS_PATH, ORIGIN, NEXT_HOP, MULTI_EXIT_DISC (MED), and communities. Of these, AS_PATH is particularly important to anomaly research because it exposes the sequence of AS numbers associated with an advertisement. Changes in path length, path composition, origin AS, or the frequency with which paths change can therefore be transformed into measurable behavioral features. Communities add another policy signal because operators use them to communicate routing intent, traffic-engineering preferences, and propagation controls (Giotsas et al., 2018; Fezeu et al., 2022).

BGP's decision process also explains why control-plane symptoms can be ambiguous. A route may change because of a physical failure, a BGP session transition, a policy modification, a newly preferred path, a more-specific advertisement, or an unauthorized origin. Withdrawals can trigger path exploration, during which routers successively advertise alternate paths before reaching a stable state. Classic work on Internet routing instability demonstrated that convergence can generate substantial update activity even when no malicious event has occurred (Labovitz et al., 2000). For anomaly-detection research, this means that update volume alone is an incomplete indicator: benign convergence and security incidents can occupy overlapping regions of the observable feature space.

Empirical BGP research depends heavily on route collectors. RouteViews and the RIPE NCC Routing Information Service (RIS) maintain distributed collectors that receive routes from participating networks and archive routing table snapshots and UPDATE streams in MRT-compatible formats. These archives enable retrospective reconstruction of incidents and longitudinal measurement of route visibility. BGPStream provides an abstraction layer for accessing and processing such data, while tools such as BML have been developed to simplify the construction of BGP datasets for machine-learning experiments (Hoarau et al., 2021). The availability of public control-plane archives has therefore transformed BGP research from small laboratory experiments into studies based on Internet-scale observations.

Route collector data nevertheless represent a sampled view of the routing system rather than a complete ground truth. Visibility depends on collector placement, participating peers, routing policy, and the routes exported to each monitor. A route visible at one collector may be absent or may appear at a different time at another. This limitation matters when building event windows and comparing incidents. The present study uses RouteViews consistently for BGP UPDATE collection; the methodological rationale and observed archive-timing considerations that led to that choice are described in Chapter 3. In the literature review, the important point is that both RouteViews and RIS are measurement infrastructures whose observations are shaped by vantage-point coverage and collector behavior.

Dataset construction is itself a substantive research problem. Fonseca et al. (2019) and Hoarau et al. (2021) illustrate the need to transform raw routing records into structured observations that can support statistical or machine-learning analysis. Typical derived variables include announcement and withdrawal counts, ratios, unique prefixes, unique ASes, AS-path length statistics, origin changes, and temporal rates. Later studies extend this representation with graph structure, AS-level dynamics, or semantics-aware features (Peng et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023; Latif-Martínez et al., 2025). These approaches establish the methodological precedent for treating public BGP telemetry as a source from which behavioral features can be engineered.

A further foundational issue is the AS-level topology. The Internet's AS graph is neither random nor static. Siganos et al. (2003) showed structural regularities in AS-level topology, while Gao (2001) demonstrated that the interpretation of AS links requires business relationships, not merely graph adjacency. Consequently, two identical-length AS paths may have very different policy meaning. This insight motivates the later integration of AS-relationship information into anomaly features: path structure describes where a route traveled, whereas relationship semantics help describe whether that propagation is economically and operationally plausible.

Taken together, foundational BGP research provides three building blocks for this praxis. First, the protocol exposes observable behavioral signals through UPDATE messages and path attributes. Second, public collectors make those signals available at Internet scale. Third, AS-level topology and policy determine how those observations should be interpreted. These foundations support a feature-engineering strategy that combines raw behavioral statistics with external security and relationship context rather than treating BGP telemetry as an undifferentiated time series.

BGP Routing Incidents and Outages

The operational consequences of BGP's distributed trust and policy model are evident in a long history of routing incidents. These events range from benign convergence and connectivity disruptions to accidental route leaks, prefix hijacks, and large-scale outages. A central lesson from the literature is that similar control-plane symptoms can arise from different incident mechanisms. This many-to-one relationship between observed routing behavior and incident type makes classification and diagnosis more difficult than simply detecting that routing behavior has changed.

Routing instability is often associated with bursts of announcements and withdrawals. When a preferred route disappears, BGP speakers may explore alternative paths, generating transient advertisements and repeated UPDATE messages before convergence. Such behavior can resemble a routing incident because both can produce abrupt deviations from an established baseline. Early studies of Internet routing instability therefore remain relevant to machine-learning research: they demonstrate that UPDATE volume alone is an incomplete indicator and that benign convergence can overlap with incident-related behavior (Labovitz et al., 2000).

Misconfiguration and routing-policy errors are persistent sources of routing disruption. Incorrect prefix advertisements, missing filters, inappropriate export policies, and unintended preference changes can cause routes to propagate outside their intended scope. Route leaks are particularly instructive because the originating AS may be legitimate even though the route is propagated in a manner that violates intended routing policy. Bagnulo et al. (2022), through ASIRIA, emphasize the importance of AS-level relationship context when evaluating suspicious propagation. This distinction makes origin-only validation insufficient for many route-leak scenarios and motivates the use of policy-aware and AS-relationship features.

Prefix hijacking differs from a route leak because the observed routing behavior involves unauthorized or deceptive origination or propagation of address space. Many origin hijacks can be identified through unexpected origin changes and changes in route visibility. ARTEMIS demonstrated that control-plane monitoring and origin information can support rapid detection and mitigation of many hijacking events (Sermpezis et al., 2018). More sophisticated forged-origin attacks can preserve the legitimate origin within a manipulated AS path, making simple origin-change checks insufficient; work such as DFOH addresses this more difficult class of attack (Holterbach et al., 2024). The evolution from straightforward origin hijacks to forged-origin scenarios illustrates why multiple routing signals are needed to characterize BGP security incidents.

Hijacks and route leaks can also interact with more-specific routing. Because forwarding decisions use longest-prefix matching, an unauthorized more-specific route may attract traffic even when a covering aggregate remains correctly originated. RPKI and Route Origin Validation (ROV) can provide important evidence in such cases when Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) accurately describe the authorized origin and maximum prefix length. However, an RPKI INVALID state is not by itself proof of malicious activity because configuration errors, stale ROAs, or incorrect maximum-length authorization can also produce invalid states (Xu et al., 2019). RPKI/ROV evidence should therefore be interpreted together with behavioral and path-context information rather than treated as a definitive incident label.

Routing outages introduce a different but overlapping control-plane pattern. Loss of upstream connectivity, BGP session failure, or other reachability disruptions can generate withdrawals, path substitutions, reduced visibility, and temporary or sustained loss of reachable prefixes without an unauthorized route advertisement. In multihomed enterprise environments, such behavior is operationally important because external reachability depends on the availability and convergence of BGP paths across multiple providers. These withdrawal- and visibility-oriented patterns can overlap with route recovery, policy changes, or other routing disturbances, making contextual and temporal evidence important when distinguishing outages from hijacks and leaks.

The incident literature also demonstrates the importance of event-level context. A single BGP UPDATE is rarely sufficient to characterize an incident. Investigators instead examine behavior across a period of time, compare route origins and paths, identify affected prefixes and ASes, evaluate changes in visibility, and consult external routing context. Systems such as BEAR seek to automate aspects of BGP event analysis and reporting, while semantics-aware approaches such as BEAM move toward interpreting the structure and context of routing anomalies rather than merely generating alerts (Chen et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). These directions are consistent with the broader operational goal of transforming BGP telemetry into information that can assist network engineers during incident investigation.

For the present study, this literature motivates the hypothesis that Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents are distinguishable not by a single deterministic indicator, but by combinations of behavioral, route-origin validation, and AS-policy signals. Hijacks are expected to be particularly associated with origin-related and RPKI/ROV evidence; route leaks with AS-path propagation, relationship sequences, and valley-free behavior; and outages with withdrawal, visibility, and path-instability characteristics. These signals are not treated as fixed rules. Instead, they provide complementary evidence that can be learned and combined by a probabilistic machine-learning classifier to classify and rank BGP incident types.

BGP Security Mechanisms and Routing Validation

BGP's original design does not cryptographically validate either an Autonomous System's authority to originate a prefix or the authenticity of the AS path contained in an UPDATE message. Routing-security research has therefore developed mechanisms that introduce verifiable information into the interdomain routing system. Among the most significant are the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) and Route Origin Validation (ROV), which provide a framework for validating whether an AS is authorized to originate a prefix, and BGPsec, which was designed to provide cryptographic validation of AS-path propagation (Gilad et al., 2017; Rodday et al., 2024). These mechanisms address different aspects of routing security: RPKI/ROV primarily provides route-origin authorization and validation, whereas BGPsec is intended to provide AS-path validation. This distinction is important to the present study because historical RPKI/ROV information is incorporated as contextual evidence for BGP incident
Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI)

The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) is a specialized public-key infrastructure designed to provide cryptographically verifiable information about Internet number resources. It enables holders of IP address space and Autonomous System (AS) numbers to publish signed objects through a hierarchical trust structure anchored in the Regional Internet Registries. In routing security, one of the most important RPKI objects is the Route Origin Authorization (ROA), which specifies whether an AS is authorized to originate a particular IP prefix. RPKI therefore provides an external source of routing authorization information that is independent of the BGP UPDATE message itself.

The security value of RPKI has been accompanied by extensive research into its deployment and operational effectiveness. Gilad et al. (2017) examined barriers to RPKI adoption and demonstrated how partial deployment limits the protection that origin validation can provide across the Internet. Chung et al. (2019) subsequently documented continued growth in RPKI deployment while also identifying operational issues associated with invalid route origins. More recent measurement studies have examined ROA coverage, ROV enforcement, repository resilience, relying-party behavior, and deployment incentives (Rodday et al., 2024). Collectively, this literature demonstrates the increasing operational relevance of RPKI while also cautioning against treating its coverage or validation outcomes as complete indicators of routing correctness or malicious activity.

RPKI also introduces infrastructure, availability, and governance considerations. Successful validation depends on the availability and correctness of repositories, certificate chains, published objects, and relying-party validation software. Heilman et al. (2014) examined transparency and trust concerns within the RPKI architecture, emphasizing that the security infrastructure itself requires mechanisms for accountability and reliable operation. Consequently, an RPKI-derived validation result should be interpreted as evidence about route-origin authorization at a particular point in time, rather than as definitive evidence that a routing announcement is benign or malicious.

This distinction is particularly relevant to the present study. Historical RPKI information is used as contextual evidence alongside BGP behavioral and AS-relationship features. Because ROAs and RPKI coverage change over time, the study evaluates observed prefix-origin pairs against historical RPKI state corresponding to the time of each BGP observation, rather than against current authorization data. This temporal alignment allows RPKI/ROV information to contribute to incident classification while preserving the routing-security context that existed when the incident occurred.

Route Origin Authorization (ROA)

A Route Origin Authorization (ROA) is a cryptographically signed RPKI object that specifies which Autonomous System is authorized to originate a particular IP prefix and may also define the maximum prefix length that the authorization covers. A ROA does not directly modify BGP route selection or determine whether a route is accepted. Instead, it provides validated authorization information that a relying party can use to evaluate whether an observed prefix-origin pair is consistent with the resource holder's published authorization. This distinction between authorization and enforcement is important: a ROA provides evidence about an authorized origin, while the routing policy of the receiving network determines how that evidence influences route acceptance.

ROA information is particularly useful for BGP incident analysis because it adds security context to an observed prefix-origin relationship. When Route Origin Validation is performed, an observed route can generally be classified as VALID, INVALID, or NotFound. A route is VALID when an applicable ROA authorizes the observed origin AS and prefix length. A route is INVALID when an applicable ROA exists but the observed route conflicts with the authorization, such as when the originating AS is not authorized or the advertised prefix exceeds the ROA's permitted maximum length. A route is NotFound when no applicable ROA covers the observed prefix. Prior research has demonstrated the value of RPKI authorization information for identifying suspicious origin behavior and strengthening the analysis of potential prefix hijacks (Wählisch et al., 2012).

Importantly, an RPKI INVALID state does not necessarily indicate malicious activity or prove that a prefix hijack has occurred. Operational conditions such as outdated or incorrectly configured ROAs, address transfers, traffic-engineering practices, and prefix-length authorization errors can produce invalid states without malicious intent. Xu et al. (2019) examined false alarms associated with RPKI-invalid routes, while Chung et al. (2019) similarly demonstrated the need to interpret invalid-origin observations carefully. This limitation supports the use of ROA-derived validation states as contextual model features rather than deterministic incident labels.

This distinction directly informs the present Praxis. The RPKI/ROV feature representation preserves not only the overall validation state but also information associated with origin mismatch and maximum-length violations. These authorization signals are combined with BGP behavioral characteristics and CAIDA AS-relationship information, allowing the machine-learning model to evaluate route-origin evidence in the broader context of an observed routing incident rather than assuming that any single RPKI state determines the incident class.
Route Origin Validation (ROV)

Route Origin Validation (ROV) is the process by which an observed BGP route is evaluated against validated RPKI information to determine whether the originating Autonomous System and advertised prefix length are consistent with applicable Route Origin Authorizations. The resulting validation state is commonly expressed as VALID, INVALID, or NotFound. Networks may then use these validation states as inputs to local routing policy, for example by rejecting or de-preferencing INVALID routes. The effectiveness of ROV therefore depends on both the availability and correctness of ROAs and the extent to which networks enforce validation results through their routing policies.

Empirical research demonstrates that measuring ROV deployment is more difficult than measuring ROA publication. The existence of a ROA can be observed through the RPKI, whereas determining whether an individual network actively rejects, de-preferences, or otherwise treats INVALID routes differently requires additional measurement. Li et al. (2023), through RoVista, developed methods for measuring and analyzing ROV behavior, while Qin et al. (2024) examined real-world ROV deployment and the gap between recommended routing-security practices and observed enforcement. These studies demonstrate that ROV implementation remains heterogeneous and that observed enforcement can depend on routing policy, measurement vantage point, and experimental methodology.

For BGP incident analysis, ROV-derived information remains valuable even when enforcement is incomplete. For example, an unexpected origin that produces an INVALID origin-mismatch state provides different security evidence from an origin change involving a prefix for which no applicable ROA exists. Similarly, an INVALID result caused by a maximum-prefix-length violation provides information that differs from an unauthorized origin. Conversely, a VALID route does not establish that the complete AS path is policy compliant, nor does it eliminate the possibility of more sophisticated routing manipulation in which the legitimate origin is preserved. ROV therefore provides route-origin authorization evidence rather than complete validation of BGP routing behavior.

This complementary role is central to the present study. Historical RPKI/ROV information is combined with BGP behavioral characteristics and CAIDA AS-relationship information so that route-origin authorization can be evaluated together with path structure, routing-policy relationships, visibility, withdrawals, origin changes, and other control-plane behavior. The final feature representation includes 16 RPKI/ROV-derived features that characterize VALID, INVALID, and NotFound observations as well as specific invalidity conditions. This approach allows ROV information to contribute to BGP incident classification without treating the validation state itself as a deterministic indicator of Hijack, Leak, or Outage.
BGPsec

BGPsec extends BGP by providing cryptographic protection for AS-path propagation. RFC 8205 defines the BGPsec protocol and introduces signed path information that allows participating BGPsec speakers to verify that an AS authorized propagation of a route to the next AS in the path (Lepinski & Sriram, 2017). Conceptually, BGPsec addresses an important limitation of route-origin validation: a route may have a legitimate and RPKI-valid origin while still containing a manipulated or unauthorized propagation path. Whereas RPKI/ROV focuses primarily on who is authorized to originate a prefix, BGPsec is designed to provide stronger assurance about how the route is propagated through participating ASes.

Research on secure path validation has identified significant challenges associated with incremental deployment, routing policy, and operational overhead. Lychev et al. (2013) examined BGP security under partial deployment and demonstrated that the benefits of secure routing mechanisms depend strongly on adoption patterns and routing policies. Other research has investigated approaches for reducing the computational, cryptographic, and memory costs associated with path validation. These deployment challenges, together with the limited availability of BGPsec-protected paths in historical routing data, help explain why contemporary BGP incident-analysis systems continue to rely on observable AS-path characteristics and routing-policy context.

BGPsec is therefore relevant to this Praxis primarily as a complementary security mechanism and conceptual boundary. The study does not perform cryptographic AS-path validation and does not use BGPsec information as a model feature. Instead, it analyzes observed AS-path behavior and enriches that information with inferred CAIDA AS relationships and historical RPKI/ROV route-origin evidence. These features cannot provide the cryptographic guarantees offered by BGPsec; however, they can be applied retrospectively to historical RouteViews observations and provide practical routing-security context for the classification and ranking of BGP incidents.
Current Deployment and Challenges

The routing-security literature consistently characterizes deployment as an incremental and uneven process. RPKI coverage has expanded substantially, but ROA publication, ROV enforcement, and operational correctness remain heterogeneous across networks (Chung et al., 2019; Rodday et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2024). BGPsec deployment remains considerably more limited. The Internet therefore operates in a mixed security environment in which some prefixes have cryptographically verifiable origin authorization, some networks apply routing policy based on ROV results, and much of AS-path interpretation continues to depend on conventional routing policy, monitoring, and inferred relationship information.

Several analytical challenges follow from this partial deployment. First, routes without applicable ROAs receive a NotFound validation state and therefore provide no positive or negative origin-authorization verdict. Second, INVALID routes can result from benign operational conditions such as stale or incorrect ROAs, address transfers, or maximum-prefix-length configuration errors. Third, route-origin validation does not identify every route leak, forged-origin attack, or AS-path manipulation. Fourth, ROV enforcement is difficult to measure because routing decisions are distributed and policy dependent. Finally, RPKI and routing-policy information change over time, making temporal alignment essential when historical incidents are analyzed retrospectively.

These limitations do not reduce the analytical value of routing-security information; rather, they define how it should be interpreted. RPKI/ROV states provide contextual evidence about route-origin authorization, while AS-relationship information provides complementary evidence about routing-policy and propagation behavior. Neither source should be treated as a deterministic incident label. A machine-learning model can instead combine these signals with behavioral BGP characteristics and learn how their joint patterns differ across incident classes.

This interpretation directly supports the design of the present Praxis. Historical RPKI/ROV information is incorporated as 16 route-origin validation features, while historical CAIDA AS-relationship information contributes 14 routing-policy and path-context features. These enrichment features are combined with 44 behavioral BGP features and evaluated through controlled feature-variant and feature-family ablation. This design allows the study to determine whether routing-security and AS-policy context provide additional discriminatory information for classifying and ranking Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents beyond behavioral BGP evidence alone.

AS Relationships, Routing Policies, and Valley-Free Routing

BGP routes are shaped not only by protocol mechanics but also by economic and operational relationships among Autonomous Systems (ASes). These relationships influence which routes an AS prefers and which routes it exports to neighboring networks. Consequently, interpretation of an observed AS path requires more than path length or topology alone; it also requires policy context. The literature on AS relationships therefore provides an important external source of information, complementary to RPKI/ROV, for interpreting route propagation and identifying behavior associated with route leaks and other routing incidents.
Autonomous System Relationships

Gao (2001) established a foundational framework for inferring AS relationships from observed BGP paths. The work formalized the idea that inter-AS links can be interpreted according to business roles such as customer-provider and peer-to-peer relationships. This abstraction is important because an AS path is not simply a sequence of network identifiers; it also reflects commercial and routing-policy relationships that influence plausible route propagation.

Later research refined AS-relationship inference as Internet interconnection became more complex. Luckie et al. (2013) proposed methods for relationship and customer-cone inference without relying exclusively on maximizing valley-free paths, while Giotsas et al. (2014) examined complex AS relationships that do not always fit traditional categories. These studies demonstrate that inferred relationship data are approximations of a dynamic and partially private commercial system, but they also show that such inference remains useful for topology research, routing-policy analysis, and interpretation of BGP paths.
Customer-Provider and Peer Relationships

In a customer-provider relationship, the customer purchases transit from the provider and generally relies on that provider for connectivity toward the broader Internet. In a peer-to-peer relationship, two ASes typically exchange traffic for their respective customers without providing unrestricted transit to one another. These economic relationships produce characteristic export policies. Routes learned from customers can generally be exported broadly, whereas routes learned from providers or peers are normally exported only to customers in order to avoid providing unpaid transit.

This policy structure gives AS paths directional meaning. Counts and ratios of customer-provider and peer-to-peer transitions can therefore encode information that ordinary AS-path length does not capture. For example, a relatively short path containing an unexpected policy transition may provide stronger evidence of abnormal propagation than a longer path that remains consistent with expected relationship patterns. Such relationship-aware measurements provide a basis for converting AS-path observations into policy-context features for machine-learning analysis.
Valley-Free Routing

The valley-free model captures a widely used abstraction of economically rational interdomain route propagation. In a simplified valley-free path, propagation may move from customer to provider zero or more times, optionally traverse a peer relationship, and then move from provider to customer zero or more times. A path that moves toward a customer and subsequently returns toward another provider can create a policy 'valley' and may indicate that an AS is providing transit contrary to expected export behavior.

Valley-free routing is a useful abstraction rather than an absolute rule. Giotsas and Zhou (2012) analyzed valley-free violations using BGP community information and demonstrated that real routing can contain exceptions and complexities. Complex business relationships, partial transit arrangements, route-server behavior, and imperfect relationship inference can all produce apparent violations. Nevertheless, valley-free behavior remains particularly relevant to route-leak analysis because leaks frequently involve propagation beyond the scope implied by customer-provider and peer relationships.

For this Praxis, valley-free violations are therefore treated as statistical evidence rather than deterministic rules. This treatment parallels the use of RPKI/ROV evidence: both provide semantically meaningful routing context while allowing for benign exceptions, incomplete coverage, and measurement uncertainty. Their value lies in how they contribute, together with behavioral BGP observations, to distinguishing among competing incident classes.
CAIDA Relationship Inference

The Center for Applied Internet Data Analysis (CAIDA) operationalizes decades of AS-level measurement research by publishing inferred AS-relationship and topology datasets. These data provide a practical mechanism for mapping adjacent AS pairs in observed BGP paths to inferred relationship categories. The methodology is grounded in research such as Gao (2001), Luckie et al. (2013), and Giotsas et al. (2014), while recognizing that no inference system has complete visibility into private interconnection agreements.

CAIDA relationship data are particularly useful for retrospective BGP studies because they can be joined with historical AS_PATH observations without requiring access to private router configurations. Once path adjacencies are mapped to inferred relationship types, features can be derived to characterize relationship composition, unknown relationships, policy-transition patterns, and valley-free behavior. This creates a bridge between publicly observable BGP telemetry and policy-aware feature engineering.

The use of inferred relationships also requires methodological caution. Relationship snapshots should be aligned as closely as possible with the period of the observed incident, and unknown relationships should be preserved rather than forced into an unsupported category. The resulting values represent inferred routing-policy context rather than authoritative commercial agreements. In the present study, historical CAIDA relationship snapshots are therefore temporally aligned with BGP observations and used to derive 14 AS-relationship features whose contribution is evaluated through controlled feature-variant and feature-family ablation.
Policy Violations and Route Leaks

Route leaks provide one of the clearest operational connections between AS relationships and BGP incident analysis. RFC 9234 describes route leaks as propagation that violates expected routing relationships or intended route-distribution scope, such as advertising a provider- or peer-learned route in a manner that creates unintended transit. Because the route origin can remain legitimate, route-origin validation alone cannot reliably identify many leak scenarios. Relationship-aware analysis is therefore important for evaluating whether the observed propagation is consistent with expected inter-AS policy.

Research systems have demonstrated the value of relationship-aware evidence for leak analysis and localization. ASIRIA uses inferred AS-relationship information to reason about route authorization and leaked-route behavior (Bagnulo et al., 2022). RoLL uses AS-triplet and relationship-oriented information to support route-leak localization, while later work such as LeakFocus extends the analysis toward identifying where abnormal propagation originates or has the greatest impact (Xie et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2025). Collectively, these studies support the use of AS-policy semantics as informative evidence when analyzing route leaks.

These findings motivate the inclusion of AS-relationship features in the present study while also highlighting an important distinction. Many relationship-aware approaches are specialized for route-leak detection or localization, whereas this Praxis evaluates relationship-derived evidence within a broader three-class incident-classification and ranking framework. The final feature representation combines 14 CAIDA-derived relationship features with 44 behavioral BGP features and 16 RPKI/ROV features so that leak-sensitive policy evidence can be evaluated alongside origin-validation and behavioral signals associated with Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents.

BGP Anomaly Detection Techniques

BGP anomaly-detection research has progressed from statistical monitoring and handcrafted rules to supervised machine learning, streaming analysis, incident-specific systems, and topology-aware approaches. The central objective of much of this work is to identify routing observations that differ from expected behavior. Although this objective is related to the present Praxis, anomaly detection and incident classification are distinct tasks. Detection asks whether observed routing behavior is abnormal, whereas the primary system developed in this study assumes that an incident has been identified and then classifies and ranks whether the observed incident is most consistent with Hijack, Leak, or Outage.

Statistical approaches exploit the fact that routing incidents can produce changes in UPDATE frequency, withdrawal activity, path length, prefix visibility, and other aggregate measures. Such techniques are attractive because they can be computationally efficient and comparatively interpretable. Recurrence-based methods extend statistical analysis to temporal structure. Al-Musawi (2024) applies recurrence quantification to BGP anomalies, while Scott et al. (2025) frame BGP anomaly detection as a multidimensional group-dynamics problem. These approaches reinforce the value of temporal and distributional changes, but they do not necessarily provide incident-level classification among competing BGP incident types.

Supervised machine-learning research has demonstrated that engineered BGP features can support anomaly detection and classification. Al-Rousan and Trajković (2012) applied support vector machine and hidden Markov model approaches to BGP anomaly classification, while Sanchez et al. (2019) compared machine-learning algorithms using BGP-derived features. Subsequent studies have examined alternative model families, class-balancing strategies, and dataset-construction choices. Collectively, this work establishes that supervised learning can distinguish routing behaviors when informative features and reliable labels are available, while also demonstrating that reported performance can be sensitive to feature construction, class distribution, and evaluation design.

Weakly supervised and unsupervised approaches address the scarcity of labeled routing incidents. Dong et al. (2021) proposed ISP self-operated BGP anomaly detection based on weak supervision, while Putina et al. (2018) and related streaming work explored online analysis of high-rate network telemetry. These approaches are valuable for identifying deviations when complete incident labels are unavailable, but anomaly scores or clusters generally require additional interpretation before they can provide the incident-level classification and ranking needed for operational diagnosis.

Real-time and incident-specific systems represent another important research direction. ARTEMIS combines real-time monitoring with automated mitigation for prefix hijacking (Sermpezis et al., 2018). ASIRIA applies AS-relationship information to route-leak analysis (Bagnulo et al., 2022). DFOH addresses forged-origin hijacks that can evade simpler origin-change checks (Holterbach et al., 2024). RoLL and LeakFocus focus on route-leak localization and related propagation analysis (Xie et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2025). These systems demonstrate that domain-specific routing features can support operationally meaningful analysis, but their specialization also limits direct generalization to a unified multi-class framework that must distinguish among several incident types.

Semantics-aware systems further narrow the gap between anomaly detection and incident interpretation. BEAM incorporates semantic context into BGP anomaly analysis, while BEAR focuses on event analysis and reporting (Chen et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). This direction reflects a broader movement from simple anomaly flags toward richer descriptions, localization, and operator-facing interpretation. Such work is relevant to the present study because enterprise network operators require more than an indication that routing behavior has changed; they also benefit from structured evidence about what type of routing incident is most consistent with the observed behavior.

Topology-aware methods challenge the assumption that aggregate message statistics alone are sufficient. Hoarau et al. (2021) examined graph-oriented representations for BGP machine-learning research, Peng et al. (2021) applied a graph-attention framework, and Latif-Martínez et al. (2025) explored models operating on Internet-topology representations. Graph methods can capture structural dependencies that may be lost in aggregate tabular features, although they generally introduce additional modeling complexity. For an enterprise-oriented incident-analysis system, this creates a tradeoff between representational richness, computational complexity, reproducibility, and the ability to relate model inputs to recognizable routing characteristics.

Another recurring issue is observation bias. Public route collectors do not observe every route from every AS, and collector placement, peer participation, and routing policy affect the control-plane information available to a model. Recent work has also examined the robustness of public-monitor-based hijack detection under adversarial conditions (Giaconia et al., 2025). Even outside an adversarial setting, incomplete visibility influences incident reconstruction and feature generation. This limitation reinforces the importance of data-quality gates, incident-level partitioning, leakage-safe evaluation, and conservative interpretation of model performance.

Overall, BGP anomaly-detection research provides four important foundations for this study. First, engineered BGP features contain useful predictive information. Second, protocol-aware, routing-security, and topology or policy context can add information beyond simple statistical measurements. Third, labeled datasets, class balance, and evaluation methodology strongly influence reported performance. Fourth, specialized detectors do not eliminate the need for approaches that can compare multiple plausible incident classes within a common framework. Building on these findings, the present Praxis evaluates a classification and ranking architecture that combines 44 behavioral BGP features, 14 CAIDA AS-relationship features, and 16 historical RPKI/ROV features and subsequently aggregates window-level evidence at the incident level.
