Machine Learning for Network Fault Detection and Diagnosis

Machine learning provides a mechanism for combining multiple weak or overlapping routing signals into a predictive decision. This is particularly relevant to BGP incident analysis because Hijack, Leak, and Outage events can share individual control-plane characteristics while differing in the combinations and temporal evolution of those characteristics. The literature spans statistical learning, ensemble methods, deep learning, graph-based learning, and explainable artificial intelligence. For the present Praxis, these model families are evaluated according to their suitability for structured BGP features, labeled incident data, operational reproducibility, and the ability to support incident-level classification and ranking.
Statistical Learning

Statistical learning occupies the boundary between classical thresholding and machine learning. Baseline distributions, robust statistics, clustering, recurrence measures, and probabilistic models can identify deviations without requiring deep architectures. In BGP analysis, these methods are useful because many routing incidents manifest as changes in UPDATE counts, withdrawal ratios, path-length distributions, origin behavior, or routing visibility. They can also be computationally attractive when processing large historical routing archives.

Romo-Chavero et al. (2025) illustrate a hybrid approach in which robust statistical screening is combined with machine-learning classifiers, including Random Forest and XGBoost. Recurrence-based studies similarly demonstrate that temporal structure can be represented through engineered statistical descriptors without requiring end-to-end sequence models. These approaches support the use of behavioral measurements as inputs to supervised learning while emphasizing that statistical deviation alone does not identify the incident mechanism.

The primary limitation of statistical learning for the present problem is semantic ambiguity. A statistically extreme routing event is not necessarily malicious, and a policy violation or origin anomaly may not produce the largest numerical deviation. Statistical measurements are therefore best interpreted as behavioral evidence. In this study, announcement and withdrawal activity, path instability, origin changes, prefix dynamics, and related variables provide that behavioral layer, while CAIDA AS-relationship and RPKI/ROV features add routing-policy and route-origin context.
Ensemble Learning

Tree-based ensemble methods are well suited to structured routing data because they can model nonlinear interactions, tolerate heterogeneous feature distributions, and operate effectively on engineered tabular representations. Random Forest reduces variance by combining many randomized decision trees, whereas gradient-boosting methods such as XGBoost construct trees sequentially so that later trees correct errors made by earlier ones. Both approaches have been widely used for classification problems in which relationships among features are nonlinear and potentially conditional.

BGP studies have repeatedly evaluated tree-based models. Sanchez et al. (2019) compared machine-learning algorithms for BGP anomaly detection, while more recent work has examined Random Forest, XGBoost, Extra Trees, LightGBM, CatBoost, and hybrid statistical-machine-learning approaches (Romo-Chavero et al., 2025). Graph-oriented studies also frequently derive structural measurements that are subsequently supplied to conventional classifiers, illustrating that sophisticated routing context can be represented through engineered features without requiring an end-to-end deep model (Shen et al., 2024).

Random Forest and XGBoost are particularly relevant to the present Praxis because the final feature representation is structured and tabular, consisting of behavioral, AS-relationship, and RPKI/ROV variables. Random Forest provides a strong and comparatively transparent ensemble baseline, while XGBoost offers a high-performance boosted-tree alternative capable of modeling complex interactions among the 74 final V4 features. The study therefore evaluates both algorithms empirically rather than assuming in advance that either model family is universally superior.

The literature also motivates analysis above the individual observation level. BGP incidents unfold over time, and multiple analytical windows may belong to the same underlying incident. A model that considers only isolated windows or simply averages their class probabilities can discard information about confidence, disagreement, and temporal evolution. This motivates incident-level aggregation and stacked learning, in which lower-level predictions are transformed into a higher-level representation before a final classifier produces the incident classification and ranking. In the completed Praxis, this principle is implemented through a leakage-safe XGBoost-to-XGBoost incident-level stacking architecture rather than the earlier hierarchical Random Forest design.
Deep Learning

Deep-learning approaches have been explored because BGP telemetry is sequential, high-volume, and potentially high dimensional. Recurrent neural networks and long short-term memory models can learn temporal dependencies from routing sequences, while representation-learning and generative approaches have been applied to broader time-series anomaly-detection problems (Niu et al., 2020). BGP-specific research has likewise investigated recurrent and temporal architectures for routing-security and anomaly-analysis tasks.

Deep models can be advantageous when raw sequence structure contains information that is difficult to summarize through manually engineered features. However, these benefits are accompanied by larger data requirements, additional hyperparameters, greater computational complexity, and often reduced direct interpretability. These tradeoffs are important when the number of independently labeled real-world incidents is modest even though each incident may contain many lower-level routing observations.

An earlier design of this Praxis considered a Temporal Fusion Transformer as a possible modeling component, but that architecture was not retained in the completed experimental pipeline. Deep learning remains relevant to the literature review because it represents an important direction in BGP and time-series research and helps clarify the model-selection rationale. For the available labeled incident corpus, engineered tabular features allowed direct integration of behavioral, CAIDA, and RPKI/ROV information and supported controlled ablation, grouped evaluation, and reproducible model comparison. Deep and streaming sequence models therefore remain important alternatives and future research directions rather than components of the final model.
Graph Neural Networks

Graph-based learning is a natural extension of BGP research because interdomain routing is inherently relational. Autonomous Systems can be represented as nodes, observed adjacencies as edges, and routing events as changes in paths or graph attributes over time. Hoarau et al. (2021) examined graph representations for BGP machine-learning research, while Peng et al. (2021) applied graph-attention techniques to capture structural and temporal relationships. Other studies have explored graph neural networks and topology-derived features for BGP anomaly analysis.

More recent work has moved toward direct use of Internet topology and graph-derived representations. Latif-Martínez et al. (2025) examine approaches that reduce dependence on manually curated BGP message features, while route-leak research has also used graph robustness, centrality, and relationship-oriented measurements before applying machine-learning models (Shen et al., 2024). These studies demonstrate that topology contains discriminatory information beyond simple path length or UPDATE volume.

Graph models, however, are not the only means of incorporating relational information. The present study represents AS relationships, relationship composition, and valley-free behavior explicitly as CAIDA-derived tabular features. This approach sacrifices some representational richness but provides a reproducible representation that can be combined directly with behavioral and RPKI/ROV features. Graph neural networks therefore motivate the importance of relational structure, while the final methodology uses an engineered policy-aware representation better matched to the available labeled corpus and experimental design.
Explainable AI (SHAP)

Interpretability is important when machine-learning outputs are intended to support network operations. Network engineers need to understand whether a model's behavior is consistent with technically plausible routing evidence rather than relying only on aggregate predictive accuracy. Feature-attribution methods such as SHAP provide one mechanism for estimating how input variables influence model predictions, and recent BGP anomaly research has increasingly incorporated explainability and feature-importance analysis (Kyryk et al., 2025).

SHAP is based on Shapley values from cooperative game theory and can provide both local and global feature-attribution summaries. Tree-based models are particularly compatible with efficient SHAP implementations. However, feature attribution should not be interpreted as proof that a feature caused the underlying routing incident. A high attribution value indicates that a variable influenced the model's prediction under the learned data distribution; it does not establish real-world causality.

In the present Praxis, the principal completed evidence for feature contribution comes from controlled feature-variant and feature-family ablation experiments. These experiments evaluate how predictive performance changes when CAIDA, RPKI/ROV, or specific behavioral feature families are included or removed. This provides direct empirical evidence about the contribution of feature groups to classification performance. SHAP remains a relevant post-hoc explainability technique and a potential extension for the final frozen model, but it is not required to support the completed feature-contribution findings reported in this study.

Summary of Research Gaps and Study Positioning

The reviewed literature demonstrates substantial progress in BGP measurement, routing security, AS-policy inference, anomaly detection, and machine learning. However, important gaps become apparent when these areas are considered together, particularly from the perspective of enterprise incident analysis. These gaps motivate a framework that moves beyond detecting abnormal routing behavior toward integrating multiple sources of routing evidence for incident-level classification and ranking.

The first gap is the continuing separation between anomaly detection and operational incident interpretation. Many systems determine whether routing behavior is unusual, while others specialize in detecting or localizing a particular incident type. Fewer approaches provide a common framework that compares multiple plausible BGP incident classes and produces probability-based rankings that can support an operator's investigation. This distinction is important because an anomaly alert alone does not indicate whether the observed behavior is most consistent with a Hijack, Leak, or Outage.

The second gap is the incomplete integration of routing-security context with machine-learning features. RPKI research has developed methods for measuring ROA coverage, route-origin validity, ROV deployment, and operational behavior (Chung et al., 2019; Li et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2024; Rodday et al., 2024). BGP anomaly research, however, has often emphasized message statistics, path characteristics, or learned representations. This creates an opportunity to evaluate historical RPKI/ROV validation information not merely as a routing-security control, but as contextual evidence that can be combined with behavioral BGP features in a multi-class incident classifier.

The third gap concerns AS-policy semantics. Relationship inference and route-leak research demonstrate that customer-provider and peer-to-peer relationships, valley-free behavior, and local AS relationship patterns can provide useful evidence for identifying abnormal route propagation (Gao, 2001; Luckie et al., 2013; Bagnulo et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2023). These signals are frequently used in leak-specific analysis rather than combined with route-origin validation and general behavioral BGP features within a unified classifier. Evaluating relationship-derived features across Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents provides a way to determine whether policy semantics contribute beyond their established role in route-leak analysis.

The fourth gap is methodological reproducibility and generalization across independently labeled real-world incidents. Public BGP archives contain very large numbers of UPDATE observations but comparatively fewer independently labeled routing incidents. This creates a risk that models evaluated at the message or window level may learn characteristics associated with particular incidents rather than patterns that generalize across incidents. Incident-level partitioning, grouped cross-validation, quality gates, feature ablation, and independent evaluation partitions are therefore important for demonstrating that performance reflects generalizable incident characteristics rather than row-level leakage or event-specific artifacts.

The fifth gap concerns interpretable evidence for feature contribution. Explainable-AI and feature-importance methods are increasingly used in network and BGP research, but predictive performance alone does not establish which routing-information sources materially improve incident discrimination. For an operationally motivated system, it is useful to determine whether route-origin validation, AS-policy context, withdrawal behavior, path instability, peer visibility, and other feature families contribute meaningfully to classification. The present study addresses this need primarily through controlled feature-variant and feature-family ablation, which measures performance changes when specific sources of routing evidence are added or removed. Post-hoc methods such as SHAP remain complementary approaches for future model explanation.

The sixth gap is the balance between model sophistication, available labeled data, and operational reproducibility. Deep-learning and graph-based approaches can learn complex temporal or relational representations from routing data (Peng et al., 2021; Latif-Martínez et al., 2025), but greater architectural complexity does not necessarily provide superior performance for structured tabular data. Broader machine-learning research has shown that tree-based ensemble methods remain highly competitive on many tabular classification problems (Fernández-Delgado et al., 2014; Grinsztajn et al., 2022). Random Forest and gradient-boosted trees are therefore appropriate candidates for a feature space composed of engineered behavioral, AS-relationship, and RPKI/ROV variables (Breiman, 2001; Chen & Guestrin, 2016). This motivates empirical model comparison rather than assuming that the most complex architecture is necessarily the most suitable.

A seventh gap concerns how lower-level BGP observations are transformed into an incident-level decision. Much of the literature evaluates individual observations, fixed windows, or simple aggregate statistics. However, a BGP incident can contain multiple analytical windows whose predictions evolve over time and differ in confidence. Simple averaging can discard information about probability distributions, disagreement, and temporal progression. This creates an opportunity to evaluate whether incident-level aggregation and stacked learning can preserve more of the evidence contained across an incident while maintaining leakage-safe separation among independent incidents.

This study is positioned at the intersection of these gaps. It constructs a corpus of documented real-world Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents; derives 44 behavioral features from historical RouteViews UPDATE data; enriches those observations with 14 historical CAIDA AS-relationship features and 16 historical RPKI/ROV features; and evaluates multiple feature variants, imbalance strategies, and machine-learning algorithms. Random Forest and XGBoost are compared empirically, and the final architecture uses XGBoost at both the window and incident levels. Window-level class probabilities are transformed into incident-level distributional, confidence, disagreement, and temporal meta-features, which are then used to produce final classification probabilities and a ranked ordering of the three incident classes.

The contribution is therefore not a new cryptographic routing protocol, a replacement for specialized hijack or route-leak detectors, or a claim of fully automated root-cause determination. Rather, the Praxis evaluates a reproducible AI-assisted classification and ranking framework that integrates behavioral routing evidence, AS-policy context, and route-origin validation information and determines whether incident-level aggregation can improve the interpretation of observed BGP incidents for enterprise network operations.

These variables describe observable changes in the control plane and have been widely used in BGP measurement and anomaly-detection research (Al-Rousan & Trajković, 2012; Fonseca et al., 2019; Putina et al., 2018). The second source is AS-relationship and routing-policy information. Customer-provider and peer-to-peer relationships, valley-free behavior, and related AS-path characteristics provide context for evaluating whether observed propagation is consistent with expected interdomain routing behavior (Gao, 2001; Giotsas & Zhou, 2012; Luckie et al., 2013; Bagnulo et al., 2022). This literature provides the basis for the feature-variant design evaluated in the Praxis. Behavioral BGP features establish how much incident information can be learned directly from routing telemetry. Historical CAIDA AS-relationship features are then used to determine whether routing-policy context adds discriminatory information, particularly for abnormal propagation and route leaks. Historical RPKI/ROV features provide an additional origin-authorization dimension that can help distinguish incidents involving unexpected or unauthorized origins. Feature-family ablation further evaluates the contribution of individual groups of routing evidence.

A further methodological consideration is the level at which classification decisions are made. Individual five-minute BGP windows contain useful behavioral evidence, but an incident consists of multiple observations whose predictions can vary over time. Simple averaging of window-level class probabilities can discard information about confidence, disagreement, probability distributions, and temporal evolution. Stacked learning provides a general mechanism for combining lower-level model outputs into a higher-level representation. In the final methodology, window-level XGBoost probabilities are therefore summarized into incident-level distributional, confidence, disagreement, and temporal meta-features, and a second XGBoost classifier produces the final incident classification and ranking. This architecture allows the study to preserve information across the incident while treating the incident—not the individual window—as the principal evaluation unit.

Evaluation must also extend beyond a single accuracy value. BGP incident classes can differ in difficulty, and row-level metrics can obscure whether a model generalizes across independent incidents. Precision, recall, and F1 provide class-sensitive measures of classification performance (He & Garcia, 2009; Sokolova & Lapalme, 2009), while ranking metrics such as Top-1, Top-2, and Mean Reciprocal Rank evaluate whether the correct incident class appears near the top of the model's probability ordering. ROC and precision-recall analysis remain useful for the experimental Normal-versus-Incident Stage 1 problem, particularly when evaluating threshold behavior under class imbalance (Fawcett, 2006; Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015). For the final Hijack/Leak/Outage classifier, however, the primary decision is based on the relative multiclass probabilities rather than a manually selected binary threshold.

The literature further emphasizes the need for careful evaluation design when many observations belong to the same underlying event. If windows from the same incident appear in both training and evaluation partitions, reported performance can be inflated by event-specific similarity. The methodology therefore treats incidents as independent experimental units and uses grouped cross-validation, nested evaluation for the stacked architecture, quality gates, and independent data partitions. This design is intended to measure generalization across incidents rather than memorization of windows belonging to the same event. A separate Validation partition and a previously sealed Final Holdout provide additional controls for model selection and terminal evaluation.

Interpretability remains important, but the completed study distinguishes between model explanation and empirical evidence of feature contribution. SHAP and related feature-attribution methods can explain how individual variables influence tree-model predictions (Lundberg & Lee, 2017; Lundberg et al., 2020), and such methods remain relevant for post-hoc analysis. However, the principal completed evidence for the value of CAIDA, RPKI/ROV, and behavioral feature families comes from controlled feature-variant and feature-family ablation. These experiments directly measure how predictive performance changes when feature groups are added or removed and therefore provide a reproducible basis for assessing which forms of routing evidence contribute to incident classification.

An important limitation identified throughout the literature is that public BGP telemetry cannot establish every underlying physical or configuration-level cause of a routing event. Public collectors observe routing behavior from limited vantage points, AS-relationship datasets contain inferred rather than authoritative commercial relationships, and RPKI coverage is incomplete (Luckie et al., 2013; Chung et al., 2019; Reuter et al., 2018; Rodday et al., 2024). Many BGP studies therefore reconstruct incidents using public routing observations and documented event information rather than direct access to every affected router (Orsini et al., 2016; Fonseca et al., 2020). Accordingly, the output of this Praxis should be interpreted as classification and ranking of BGP incident types based on available control-plane evidence, not as proof of the physical or organizational root cause of an incident.

The final methodological design therefore brings together several established research areas. Foundational BGP studies define the control-plane information that can be observed; RouteViews provides the historical UPDATE data used in the experimental pipeline; CAIDA relationship data provide inferred routing-policy context; and historical RPKI/ROV information provides route-origin authorization evidence. Machine-learning research motivates the comparison of Random Forest and XGBoost for the resulting structured feature space, while stacking provides a mechanism for transforming multiple window-level predictions into an incident-level decision. Research Methodology Overview

This chapter describes the methodology used to develop and evaluate the artificial intelligence–based classification and ranking system for Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) incidents. The study was designed to determine whether historical BGP control-plane observations could be transformed into structured machine-learning representations that distinguish among three operational incident classes: Hijack, Leak, and Outage. The final primary system does not treat Normal routing behavior as a fourth output class. Normal-versus-Incident discrimination was investigated separately as an experimental auxiliary problem but was not retained as a mandatory component of the final architecture.

The research followed a reproducible multi-stage data and machine-learning pipeline. Documented routing incidents were first identified and labeled, after which historical BGP UPDATE data were acquired from the University of Oregon RouteViews archive. Raw MRT records were filtered to retain incident-relevant observations and were subjected to quality-control checks before feature construction. The retained UPDATE observations were then organized into non-overlapping five-minute analytical windows. Each five-minute window served as a lower-level machine-learning observation, while each BGP incident was treated as the independent experimental unit for model development and evaluation.

Feature engineering was performed in three complementary layers. First, 44 behavioral BGP features were derived from UPDATE activity, including announcements, withdrawals, prefix dynamics, peer visibility, AS-path characteristics, origin changes, and path-instability behavior. Second, the behavioral representation was enriched with 14 historical CAIDA AS-relationship features that provided routing-policy and valley-free path context. Third, 16 historical RPKI/ROV features were added to represent route-origin authorization states and related origin-mismatch and maximum-prefix-length evidence. Together, these components formed the final V4 feature representation of 74 features per analytical window.

Model development was conducted primarily within the TRAIN partition using incident-level grouped cross-validation so that windows belonging to the same incident were not split across training and evaluation folds. The methodology evaluated multiple feature variants, imbalance-treatment strategies, Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers, hyperparameter configurations, and model-stability conditions. This controlled development process ultimately selected XGBoost as the preferred model family for the final classification architecture.

The final system uses incident-level temporal stacking. At the first level, XGBoost models generate window-level probabilities for Hijack, Leak, and Outage. These probabilities are then transformed into incident-level meta-features that summarize probability distributions, prediction confidence, disagreement among windows, and temporal behavior across early, middle, and late portions of the incident. A second XGBoost classifier uses this incident-level representation to produce the final class probabilities. The class with the highest probability becomes the Top-1 classification, while the three probabilities are ordered to produce the ranked incident output.

The methodology also incorporated several controls to reduce evaluation bias and data leakage. These included incident-level dataset partitioning, grouped and nested cross-validation, feature and model freezing, threshold-leakage controls for the experimental Normal-versus-Incident stage, multi-seed stability analysis, label-permutation testing, first- and second-level stacking leakage audits, and independent Validation and Final Holdout partitions. The Final Holdout remained sealed until the final deployable model architecture and second-level hyperparameters had been frozen.

The complete methodological workflow therefore progressed through the following stages: incident identification, RouteViews acquisition, quality control, five-minute window construction, Behavioral/CAIDA/RPKI feature engineering, model development, incident-level stacking, Validation and model freezing, and one-time Final Holdout evaluation. The following sections describe each stage in detail and explain the procedures used to maintain reproducibility, temporal consistency, and evaluation integrity throughout the study.

Research Design and Experimental Framework

This Praxis used a quantitative experimental design based on supervised machine learning to evaluate whether BGP control-plane observations could be used to classify and rank routing incidents. Historical incidents with documented labels served as the supervised learning units, and each incident was represented by a collection of routing observations gathered from the corresponding event period. The primary classification task focused on three incident classes: Hijack, Leak, and Outage. A separate Normal-versus-Incident experiment was also conducted, but it was treated as an auxiliary analysis rather than as a required stage of the final model.

The research design was selected because the study questions are empirical and measurable. The experiments evaluate whether observable BGP behavior contains sufficient information to distinguish among incident types, whether additional routing-policy and route-origin validation context improves classification, and whether incident-level aggregation of lower-level predictions improves final classification and ranking performance. These questions are addressed through controlled feature comparisons, model comparisons, grouped cross-validation, independent evaluation partitions, and final sealed Holdout testing.

The design was incident based rather than row based. This distinction is critical because multiple five-minute analytical windows from the same incident are highly related and may share prefixes, peers, AS paths, routing-policy characteristics, and temporal patterns. Randomly distributing windows from the same incident across training and evaluation sets could allow the model to learn incident-specific characteristics and later be evaluated on highly similar observations from that same event, creating an overly optimistic estimate of generalization.

To reduce this risk, the methodology treated the BGP incident as the independent experimental unit. Windows belonging to the same incident were kept within the same partition and the same cross-validation group. Model development used incident-level grouped cross-validation within the TRAIN partition, while separate Validation and Final Holdout partitions contained incidents that were not used for fitting the corresponding evaluated model. This structure was intended to measure whether the model could generalize across different incidents, rather than merely across different rows derived from the same incident.

The resulting framework therefore separates two analytical levels. At the lower level, each non-overlapping five-minute window represents a structured machine-learning observation. At the higher level, all windows associated with the same routing incident are treated as members of a single experimental group. This hierarchy supports both leakage-safe model development and the final incident-level stacking architecture, in which evidence from multiple windows is combined to produce a single classification and ranking for each BGP incident.
Experimental Unit and Analytical Observation

The methodology distinguishes between the BGP incident as the experimental unit and the five-minute analytical window as the lower-level machine-learning observation. This distinction is necessary because a single routing incident can generate many BGP UPDATE messages over time, and treating each UPDATE or feature row as an independent event would overstate the amount of independent information available for model development and evaluation.

Each documented Hijack, Leak, or Outage incident was therefore assigned a unique incident identifier and treated as an independent experimental group. Historical BGP UPDATE observations associated with the incident were organized into non-overlapping five-minute windows. Feature engineering was then performed at this window level, producing one structured feature vector for each available analytical window. Each feature vector contained behavioral BGP characteristics and, depending on the experimental feature variant, corresponding CAIDA AS-relationship and RPKI/ROV information.

Although five-minute windows served as inputs to the first-level machine-learning models, windows originating from the same incident were not considered statistically independent for dataset partitioning or cross-validation. They can share affected prefixes, Autonomous Systems, peers, AS paths, and temporal characteristics associated with the same underlying routing event. Allowing windows from a single incident to appear in both training and evaluation data could therefore create incident-level data leakage and produce an overly optimistic estimate of model generalization.

To prevent this condition, all windows associated with the same incident were kept within the same dataset partition and cross-validation group. Incident-level grouping was preserved during model development so that a model trained on one set of incidents was evaluated using different incidents rather than different windows from incidents already represented in training. This principle was maintained throughout grouped cross-validation, model comparison, hyperparameter optimization, incident-level stacking, Validation, and Final Holdout evaluation.

The distinction between analytical observations and experimental units also supports the final model architecture. At the first level, individual five-minute windows are classified to generate probabilities for Hijack, Leak, and Outage. These window-level predictions are subsequently combined into an incident-level representation that captures their distribution, confidence, disagreement, and temporal progression. The final classification and ranking are therefore produced once per incident, rather than treating each five-minute window as a separate routing incident.
Accordingly, the methodology uses two related analytical levels:
Analytical observation: one non-overlapping five-minute BGP feature window used as input to the lower-level classifier.
Experimental unit: one independently labeled BGP incident consisting of one or more associated analytical windows and used as the unit for grouping, evaluation, and final classification and ranking.

This structure ensures that the large number of BGP observations available within an incident contributes useful temporal and behavioral information without being incorrectly interpreted as an equivalent number of independent routing incidents.
Development and Evaluation Strategy

The study used separate TRAIN, Validation, and Final Holdout partitions to distinguish iterative model development from independent model evaluation. Incidents, rather than individual five-minute analytical windows, were assigned to these partitions so that observations derived from the same routing incident could not appear across development and evaluation datasets. This partitioning strategy was maintained throughout the experimental process to reduce data leakage and provide a more reliable assessment of generalization across independent BGP incidents.

The TRAIN partition served as the primary environment for feature engineering, model development, and experimental comparison. It contained 993 independently labeled incidents, consisting of 331 Hijack, 331 Leak, and 331 Outage incidents. Within TRAIN, incident-level grouped cross-validation was used to compare feature configurations, imbalance-treatment strategies, model families, hyperparameter configurations, and alternative classification architectures. Group assignments ensured that all analytical windows belonging to the same incident remained together within a cross-validation fold. As a result, development decisions were based on performance across previously unseen TRAIN incidents rather than random row-level splits.

A separate Validation partition contained 213 incidents, consisting of 71 Hijack, 71 Leak, and 71 Outage incidents. Validation remained isolated during the primary TRAIN development process and was accessed only after a model candidate and evaluation protocol had been predefined. Its purpose was to provide an independent confirmation of whether the selected TRAIN-developed model generalized to incidents outside the development partition. Feature definitions, model parameters, and evaluation criteria were not modified in response to the Validation results.

Following the initial Validation evaluation, additional architecture research was conducted as a versioned TRAIN-only development phase. This subsequent work did not reuse the Validation partition for model selection. Instead, architecture comparisons and verification procedures continued to use TRAIN data through grouped and nested cross-validation. This preserved the separation between the previously observed Validation results and the development of the later incident-level architecture.

The Final Holdout partition served as the terminal independent evaluation dataset. It contained 213 incidents, equally distributed across 71 Hijack, 71 Leak, and 71 Outage incidents. The Final Holdout remained sealed throughout feature development, model comparison, hyperparameter optimization, Validation, subsequent TRAIN-only architecture development, stability analysis, and final model freezing. Before the Final Holdout was accessed, the final feature schema, model architecture, inference procedure, and deployable hyperparameters were fixed and subjected to a pre-access audit.
The overall development and evaluation strategy can therefore be summarized as:

TRAIN development and grouped cross-validation → independent Validation confirmation → versioned TRAIN-only architecture development and verification → final model freeze → one-time Final Holdout evaluation.

This strategy maintained a clear distinction between model development, independent confirmation, and terminal generalization assessment. Most importantly, the Final Holdout incidents were not used to select features, tune hyperparameters, choose the final architecture, or modify the model after evaluation.
Experimental Environment and Implementation Platform

The full experiment was implemented in Databricks Serverless Interactive compute running on Amazon Web Services. The environment was CPU backed and provided four logical CPUs and 30.8 GB of RAM. Python 3.12.3 was used with scikit-learn 1.6.1, NumPy 2.1.3, pandas 2.2.3, and joblib 1.4.2. No GPU was required for the final Random Forest pipeline.

Computational and memory considerations influenced several implementation choices throughout the experimental pipeline. Large BGP datasets and intermediate enrichment artifacts were stored primarily in Parquet format to support efficient columnar storage, reduced disk usage, and selective loading during feature engineering and model development. Where appropriate, numerical feature representations used memory-efficient data types to reduce processing overhead. Computationally intensive operations, including CAIDA and RPKI/ROV enrichment, were also designed to reuse previously processed evidence and cached historical data rather than repeatedly parsing the underlying MRT archives.

Model development was structured to preserve experimental integrity while remaining computationally practical. Random Forest and XGBoost experiments used incident-level grouped folds, and later hyperparameter searches were bounded to predefined candidate spaces. Multi-seed stability analysis was applied only to shortlisted model configurations rather than every candidate. These choices reduced unnecessary computation while preserving the incident-level grouping and evaluation procedures required by the research design.

Intermediate and final artifacts were persisted throughout the pipeline so that later experimental stages could reuse verified outputs without repeating earlier data-processing steps. These artifacts included CSV, YAML, JSON, Parquet, model-configuration, notebook, figure, and audit outputs, together with frozen feature schemas and experiment registries. The artifact-based workflow provided traceability across feature engineering, model comparison, ablation, Validation, and Final Holdout evaluation.

Importantly, computational reuse did not include repeated evaluation against the Final Holdout. Model development and comparison were conducted primarily within the TRAIN partition using grouped and nested cross-validation. Validation was accessed under a controlled confirmation protocol, and the Final Holdout remained sealed until the final architecture, feature representation, inference procedure, and deployable hyperparameters had been frozen. This separation allowed previously generated data-processing artifacts to be reused for computational efficiency without compromising the independence of the final evaluation.
Multi-Source Incident Corpus Construction

The incident corpus was constructed from multiple documented sources to reduce dependence on a single incident list and to provide broader variation across time, networks, and routing conditions. Historical BGP incidents were assembled from previously curated records and publicly documented routing events. For each incident, available metadata such as the incident date, affected prefix or prefixes, involved Autonomous Systems (ASes), incident type, and source reference were standardized before the incident was admitted to the experimental pipeline.

The final labeled corpus contained 1,419 independent BGP incidents, equally distributed across the three target classes: 473 Hijack, 473 Leak, and 473 Outage incidents. These incidents were subsequently divided at the incident level into 993 TRAIN incidents, 213 Validation incidents, and 213 Final Holdout incidents. Each partition preserved an equal class distribution, and no incident was permitted to appear in more than one partition.

Corpus construction evolved throughout the development of the Praxis. Earlier versions of the study used a substantially smaller manually curated incident set, including an initial 84-event candidate manifest that was subjected to data-quality review. As the research progressed, the corpus was expanded and standardized to provide a larger and more balanced collection of independently labeled incidents. The earlier event sets were retained as historical development artifacts, while the final partitioned corpus became the authoritative dataset for model development and evaluation.

A structured incident manifest served as the control record for the data-processing pipeline. The manifest linked each incident to its unique identifier, class label, event date, source provenance, affected routing information where available, partition assignment, and processing status. It also supported the tracking of duplicate records, unavailable routing data, quality-gate outcomes, and incidents requiring additional review. Rather than silently discarding problematic incidents, their status and disposition were recorded so that corpus construction remained auditable and reproducible.

An important distinction was maintained between incident-source information and the BGP telemetry used for feature generation. Public incident reports and curated event records were used to establish incident identity and labeling, whereas the historical BGP UPDATE observations used to construct the machine-learning features were obtained from RouteViews. Additional external datasets, including CAIDA AS-relationship information and historical RPKI/ROV data, were subsequently used as contextual feature-enrichment sources rather than as incident-labeling sources.

This multi-source approach was intended to reduce event-specific bias and expose the models to incidents spanning different networks, routing environments, and historical periods. By treating each documented incident as an independent experimental unit and preserving source provenance throughout the pipeline, the methodology established a traceable foundation for subsequent BGP data acquisition, quality control, feature engineering, model development, and independent evaluation.
Incident Labeling and Dataset Partitioning

Each incident in the final corpus was assigned one of three target labels: Hijack, Leak, or Outage. Labels were derived from the documented incident classification and associated source information maintained in the incident manifest. Labeling was performed at the incident level, meaning that all five-minute analytical windows generated from the same incident inherited the same incident-class label. This preserved the relationship between lower-level BGP observations and the independently labeled routing event from which they were derived.

The final corpus contained 1,419 labeled incidents, with an equal distribution of 473 Hijack, 473 Leak, and 473 Outage incidents. The corpus was partitioned into three mutually exclusive datasets: TRAIN, Validation, and Final Holdout. Partitioning was performed using the incident identifier rather than individual feature rows so that all observations associated with an incident remained within a single partition.

The TRAIN partition contained 993 incidents, consisting of 331 Hijack, 331 Leak, and 331 Outage incidents. TRAIN served as the primary development partition and was used for feature evaluation, imbalance-treatment experiments, model comparison, hyperparameter optimization, grouped cross-validation, and subsequent incident-level architecture development.

The Validation partition contained 213 incidents, consisting of 71 Hijack, 71 Leak, and 71 Outage incidents. Validation was isolated from the primary TRAIN development process and was accessed under a predefined confirmation protocol. Its purpose was to provide an independent assessment of the selected TRAIN-developed model before subsequent versioned architecture development.

The Final Holdout partition also contained 213 incidents, consisting of 71 Hijack, 71 Leak, and 71 Outage incidents. The Final Holdout remained sealed throughout feature engineering, model development, hyperparameter optimization, Validation, subsequent TRAIN-only architecture experiments, stability analysis, and final model freezing. It was accessed only after the final feature schema, model architecture, inference procedure, and deployable hyperparameters had been fixed.
