The incident-level partitioning strategy was an important control against data leakage. A single BGP incident can generate many five-minute analytical windows that share affected prefixes, Autonomous Systems, peers, AS paths, and temporal characteristics. If windows from the same incident were distributed across different partitions, the model could be trained and evaluated on highly related observations from the same underlying event, potentially producing an overly optimistic estimate of generalization.

To prevent this condition, an incident was assigned to exactly one partition, and all analytical windows associated with that incident remained within that partition. Within TRAIN, the same principle was applied during grouped cross-validation so that all windows from a given incident remained in the same fold. Consequently, model performance was evaluated across independent incidents rather than across randomly separated rows from the same routing event.

This partitioning framework established the evaluation boundary used throughout the remainder of the study and provided the foundation for leakage-safe feature engineering, model development, Validation, and Final Holdout evaluation.
BGP UPDAGE Data Collection via RouteViews

Historical BGP UPDATE data used in this study were obtained from the University of Oregon RouteViews archive. RouteViews maintains distributed BGP collectors that receive routing information from participating networks and preserve historical routing-table and UPDATE data in Multi-Threaded Routing Toolkit (MRT) format. These archives provided the control-plane observations used to reconstruct the routing behavior associated with the documented Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents in the corpus.

Data acquisition was performed on an incident-specific basis rather than by downloading the complete RouteViews archive. Each incident record contained temporal and routing metadata that identified the period of interest and, where available, the affected prefixes and Autonomous Systems. These metadata were used to determine the RouteViews files required to cover the configured observation period surrounding each incident. This approach reduced unnecessary processing while preserving sufficient pre-event and in-event routing information for subsequent feature construction.

RouteViews publishes UPDATE data from multiple collectors and historical periods. Collector and archive availability were therefore verified before incident processing. The retrieval pipeline resolved the appropriate archive locations and identified the MRT files corresponding to each incident observation period. Downloaded files were tracked so that previously retrieved data could be reused rather than downloaded repeatedly during later processing stages. Duplicate file references and unavailable archive objects were also recorded to maintain a reproducible acquisition history.

The raw RouteViews data were stored in compressed MRT format and required parsing before machine-learning features could be generated. During parsing, BGP UPDATE records were converted into structured observations containing the routing attributes required by the behavioral feature pipeline. Relevant information included timestamps, announcements and withdrawals, advertised prefixes, peer information, origin Autonomous Systems, AS paths, and available BGP path attributes. Records were then filtered according to the routing information associated with the corresponding incident so that unrelated global BGP activity did not dominate the incident representation.

Each incident was processed across its configured observation window, and the resulting BGP observations were subsequently assigned to non-overlapping five-minute analytical windows. The purpose of the incident observation period was to capture the evolution of routing behavior associated with the event, while the five-minute windows provided a consistent lower-level temporal unit for feature engineering and machine-learning analysis. The exact five-minute window construction procedure is described in Section 3.8.

Because the corpus covered a large number of incidents and historical periods, RouteViews retrieval and MRT processing were performed in controlled batches rather than as a single monolithic operation. Batch processing reduced memory and storage pressure, allowed completed work to be preserved incrementally, and made individual incidents easier to recover when downloads or parsing operations failed. Processing state was recorded so that successful incidents did not need to be repeated when a subset of files required additional retrieval or processing.

The pipeline also included recovery procedures for incomplete or unavailable data. Missing archive files, insufficient incident-relevant observations, parsing failures, or other data-quality conditions were recorded rather than silently ignored. Where appropriate, affected files or incidents were retried using the verified RouteViews archive path or reprocessed from previously downloaded MRT data. Incidents that continued to lack sufficient supporting BGP observations were passed to the data-quality process described in Section 3.7 for review and disposition.

A further design objective was to avoid unnecessary repeated parsing of the large historical MRT corpus. Intermediate structured and compact evidence artifacts were persisted after successful processing and reused during later feature-enrichment stages where possible. This was particularly important for historical CAIDA and RPKI/ROV enrichment, which could operate on previously extracted routing evidence without requiring the complete RouteViews corpus to be reparsed for every experiment.

RouteViews therefore served a specific role in the experimental pipeline: it provided the historical BGP control-plane observations used to construct the behavioral representation of each incident. Incident documentation supplied the event identity and labels, while CAIDA and historical RPKI data were incorporated separately as contextual enrichment sources. Maintaining this separation among incident provenance, BGP telemetry, and external enrichment data supported a reproducible and auditable feature-engineering process.
Pre-Training Data Quality Gates

Before feature engineering and model development, the incident corpus was subjected to a pre-training data-quality gate to determine whether each incident had sufficient and reliable BGP evidence for inclusion in the experimental pipeline. The purpose of this process was to prevent incidents with incomplete metadata, unavailable routing archives, insufficient relevant BGP observations, or other processing problems from being treated as equivalent to fully supported incidents.

Quality assessment was performed at the incident level. Each incident was evaluated using its manifest metadata, RouteViews retrieval status, parsing results, and the availability of incident-relevant BGP observations. The quality gate therefore occurred before model fitting and was independent of model performance. An incident was not retained or removed because a classifier predicted it correctly or incorrectly; its disposition depended only on the availability and integrity of the underlying data.

The quality-control process examined several conditions. First, the incident required a valid class label, event date, and sufficient routing information to support historical data retrieval. Second, the required RouteViews MRT data had to be available for the configured observation period. Third, the MRT files had to parse successfully and produce usable BGP observations. Fourth, the resulting observations had to contain sufficient incident-relevant routing information for five-minute feature construction. Finally, generated feature rows were checked for schema consistency, missing values, invalid numerical values, and other conditions that could compromise downstream model development.

Incidents were assigned explicit quality dispositions rather than being silently included or discarded. The principal dispositions were PASS, REVIEW, FAIL, HOLDOUT, and REMOVED. PASS indicated that the incident satisfied the required data-quality criteria and could proceed through the pipeline. REVIEW identified an incident that required additional inspection or recovery before a final decision. FAIL indicated that one or more required quality conditions were not satisfied. HOLDOUT identified incidents intentionally reserved from model development under the partitioning strategy, while REMOVED documented incidents that were excluded from the usable corpus together with the reason for exclusion.

When a quality issue could be corrected without changing the incident definition or label, the pipeline used a recovery process. Examples included retrying unavailable RouteViews files, correcting archive-path resolution, reprocessing failed MRT files, or regenerating intermediate artifacts. Successful recovery returned the incident to the quality gate for reevaluation. This procedure distinguished recoverable processing failures from genuine absence of usable routing evidence and avoided excluding incidents solely because of temporary acquisition or processing errors.

Quality controls were also applied after feature construction. The behavioral feature matrices were checked for expected row counts, schema consistency, and feature integrity before they were frozen for modeling. Similar audits were performed after CAIDA and RPKI/ROV enrichment to verify that the enrichment process did not alter the previously frozen behavioral values. This resulted in explicit corpus and feature-quality audit artifacts that documented whether each stage satisfied its predefined integrity requirements.

The quality-gate methodology was especially important because the study used historical public routing data collected across different time periods and RouteViews collectors. Archive availability, collector visibility, and the amount of incident-relevant routing evidence can vary substantially among incidents. Treating these differences explicitly reduced the risk that missing or incomplete observations would be interpreted as meaningful routing behavior by the machine-learning models.

The resulting quality-control process established a traceable boundary between incident identification and model-ready data. Only incidents and feature representations that satisfied the required quality and integrity checks proceeded to controlled model development, while review, recovery, and exclusion decisions remained documented for reproducibility and later audit.
Five-Minute Analytical Window Construction

Following MRT parsing and incident-relevance filtering, the retained BGP UPDATE observations were organized into non-overlapping five-minute analytical windows. The purpose of this step was to transform variable-rate BGP message streams into a consistent temporal representation suitable for feature engineering and machine-learning analysis. Rather than treating every individual UPDATE message as an independent observation, all incident-relevant routing activity occurring within the same five-minute interval was summarized into a structured feature vector.

The five-minute interval provides a practical balance between temporal resolution and evidence accumulation. BGP UPDATE activity can be highly bursty, and individual announcements or withdrawals may reflect transient convergence behavior rather than the broader characteristics of an incident. Aggregating observations over a short temporal interval allows related routing activity to be characterized collectively while preserving sufficient temporal resolution to observe changes as an incident develops.

The use of five-minute aggregation is also supported by prior BGP research. Deshpande et al. (2009) extracted BGP instability features at five-minute intervals in an online instability-detection framework, including announcement and withdrawal volumes, AS-path length, and AS-path edit-distance measurements. Their work demonstrates established precedent for representing BGP control-plane behavior as five-minute feature time series. Similarly, Fonseca et al. (2019) generated machine-learning datasets using 1-, 5-, and 10-minute time bins, demonstrating that five-minute aggregation is an established temporal resolution for transforming BGP observations into structured machine-learning features. These studies provide methodological support for the five-minute interval used in the present Praxis without implying that five minutes is universally optimal for all BGP-analysis tasks.

For each incident, UPDATE timestamps were aligned to the corresponding five-minute interval, and observations falling within the same interval were grouped together before behavioral feature calculation. The resulting analytical windows retained the temporal ordering of the incident while providing a common unit from which announcement, withdrawal, prefix, peer, origin, and AS-path characteristics could be calculated. Windows containing different numbers of raw UPDATE observations therefore produced feature vectors with the same schema, allowing incidents of different sizes and UPDATE volumes to be processed consistently.

Each five-minute window was assigned a unique window identifier and remained associated with its parent incident identifier. This relationship was preserved throughout feature engineering, enrichment, model development, and evaluation. Although the five-minute windows served as lower-level machine-learning observations, they were not treated as statistically independent incidents. All windows belonging to the same incident remained within the same dataset partition and cross-validation group to prevent incident-level leakage.

The five-minute representation also provided the temporal basis for subsequent CAIDA and RPKI/ROV enrichment. Historical contextual information was aligned with the corresponding observation period so that AS-relationship and route-origin validation evidence reflected the routing context available at or near the time of the incident. The resulting Behavioral, CAIDA, and RPKI/ROV values were then combined into the feature variants described later in this chapter.

The selected window size represents a methodological design choice rather than a claim that five minutes is the minimum time required to classify a BGP incident. The final system was trained and evaluated using complete five-minute analytical windows, and its results should therefore be interpreted within that temporal representation. Sub-five-minute classification would require reconstruction and evaluation of features at finer temporal resolutions and is outside the scope of the present study. Incremental or streaming feature computation at shorter observation intervals is identified as an area for future research.
Behavioral Feature Engineering

Following construction of the five-minute analytical windows, the next stage transformed the BGP UPDATE observations within each window into a structured set of behavioral features. The purpose of behavioral feature engineering was to characterize how routing behavior changed during an incident using information observable directly from the BGP control plane. These features formed the foundation of the machine-learning representation before external CAIDA AS-relationship and RPKI/ROV information was added.

The final behavioral representation contained 44 features per five-minute analytical window. Rather than relying on a single indicator such as UPDATE volume, the feature set captured multiple dimensions of routing activity. This design was motivated by the fact that Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents can produce overlapping individual symptoms. For example, increased UPDATE activity may occur during both an outage and a hijack, while AS-path changes may occur during route leaks, convergence, or ordinary routing-policy changes. The behavioral representation therefore used combinations of measurements to characterize each analytical window.
The 44 behavioral features were organized into eight functional families:
Announcement and UPDATE activity — features characterizing the volume and distribution of BGP announcements and overall UPDATE activity within the analytical window.
Withdrawal activity — features measuring route withdrawals and withdrawal-related behavior that may indicate loss of reachability, convergence, or routing instability.
Prefix dynamics — features describing the number, diversity, and behavior of prefixes observed during the window, including changes in prefix-level routing activity.
Peer and visibility behavior — features characterizing the number and diversity of BGP peers observing or advertising relevant routing information and changes in routing visibility.
AS-path length and structure — features describing characteristics of observed AS paths, including path length, structural variation, and related path properties.
AS-path instability and path change — features measuring changes in AS-path observations across the analytical period and the degree to which routing paths changed or became unstable.
Origin change and multi-origin behavior — features characterizing changes in the originating AS and the presence of multiple origins associated with the same prefix.
AS-path prepending — features describing repeated AS numbers within observed paths, which may reflect traffic-engineering behavior or changes in routing preference.

The feature-engineering process aggregated all incident-relevant BGP observations occurring within the same five-minute interval. Count-based features measured the frequency of particular routing behaviors, while ratio, diversity, and statistical features normalized or summarized those observations so that analytical windows with different UPDATE volumes could still be compared. Missing or unavailable observations were handled according to the predefined feature-generation policy rather than being interpreted automatically as evidence of a particular incident class.

Each resulting behavioral feature row retained its window identifier, incident identifier, class label, and temporal position within the parent incident. These identifiers were used for provenance, grouping, and later incident-level aggregation but were not treated as predictive model features. Maintaining this separation prevented incident identity or class metadata from entering the model input while preserving the information necessary for grouped cross-validation and leakage auditing.

The behavioral feature schema was frozen before external enrichment was applied. This produced the V1 feature variant, consisting exclusively of the 44 behavioral features. V1 served as the behavioral baseline against which subsequent enrichment could be evaluated. The same behavioral values and feature ordering were preserved when CAIDA and RPKI/ROV information were added, ensuring that differences among feature variants reflected the added contextual information rather than changes to the underlying behavioral representation.

Behavioral feature engineering therefore established the primary representation of observed BGP activity used throughout the study. CAIDA AS-relationship and RPKI/ROV enrichment, described in subsequent sections, supplemented this representation with routing-policy and route-origin authorization context. This separation enabled controlled ablation experiments to determine how much predictive information was provided by behavioral BGP observations alone and how much additional information was contributed by the external enrichment sources.
Normal Ground-Truth Construction

Although the primary classification task of the Praxis focused on Hijack, Leak, and Outage, the research also investigated whether BGP observations could first be distinguished as Normal or Incident behavior. Conducting this experiment required a Normal reference corpus that was constructed independently of the labeled incident observations. Normal windows could not simply be defined as periods outside the documented incident interval because the absence of a known incident label does not guarantee that routing behavior was stable or unaffected by another event.

A controlled Normal ground-truth construction process was therefore developed using historical BGP routing evidence. The process combined candidate-period selection, Routing Information Base (RIB) evidence, BGP UPDATE activity, and explicit qualification criteria. The objective was to identify comparison windows that represented observable routing behavior without evidence of the target incident conditions while avoiding assumptions that an arbitrary quiet period was necessarily Normal.

The Normal corpus was used only for the experimental Normal-versus-Incident Stage 1 analyses. It was not added as a fourth class to the final Hijack/Leak/Outage classification and ranking architecture. This distinction allowed the study to evaluate anomaly-screening behavior separately without changing the definition of the primary incident-classification problem.
Normal Candidate Selection

Normal candidate periods were selected from historical routing intervals associated with the available incident context but outside the target incident activity used for the labeled incident observations. Candidate selection was performed using predefined temporal and routing criteria rather than by searching for periods that produced favorable model performance.

Each candidate period retained provenance linking it to the corresponding routing context and source data. Candidate windows were also assigned identifiers separate from the incident identifiers used for labeled Hijack, Leak, and Outage observations. This allowed Normal observations to be tracked independently while preserving sufficient information to prevent related Normal and incident observations from being separated improperly during grouped model evaluation.

Candidate selection represented only the first step of the Normal qualification process. A candidate was not considered verified Normal merely because it occurred outside a documented incident interval. Additional evidence from historical routing state and UPDATE activity was required before the candidate could be admitted to the frozen Normal corpus.
RIB-Assisted Prescreening

Historical Routing Information Base (RIB) information was used as a prescreening mechanism to evaluate the routing state surrounding each Normal candidate period. RIB snapshots provide a broader view of the routes visible to a collector at a particular point in time and therefore complement the event-driven information contained in BGP UPDATE streams.

The prescreening process examined whether the routing context associated with a candidate period was sufficiently observable and consistent for further evaluation. RIB evidence was used to establish the presence and routing context of relevant prefixes and paths before UPDATE-based qualification was performed. Candidate periods lacking sufficient supporting routing-state information could therefore be rejected or flagged for review before entering the more detailed qualification stage.

RIB-assisted prescreening reduced the risk of treating a period as Normal simply because few UPDATE messages were observed. A low level of UPDATE activity may indicate stable routing, but it may also result from limited collector visibility or insufficient evidence. Combining routing-state information with subsequent UPDATE analysis provided a more defensible basis for Normal ground-truth construction.
UPDATE-Based Qualification

Candidates that passed RIB-assisted prescreening were subsequently evaluated using historical BGP UPDATE observations. The qualification process examined the routing activity within the candidate period to determine whether the available evidence was consistent with its use as a Normal comparison window.

UPDATE-based qualification considered the behavioral characteristics available from the same historical routing infrastructure used for incident processing. Candidate periods exhibiting evidence inconsistent with the predefined Normal criteria were excluded or flagged for review rather than automatically accepted. This prevented the Normal corpus from being defined solely by the absence of a documented Hijack, Leak, or Outage label.

The combination of RIB and UPDATE evidence provided two complementary perspectives. RIB information established routing-state context, while UPDATE observations characterized routing changes occurring within the candidate interval. A candidate was retained only when the available evidence satisfied the qualification requirements established for the Normal corpus.

The qualification process was completed before Stage 1 model evaluation. Normal windows were therefore not selected according to whether a classifier could recognize them successfully. This separation was necessary to prevent model performance from influencing the construction of the Normal ground truth.
Frozen Normal Corpus

After candidate selection, RIB-assisted prescreening, and UPDATE-based qualification were completed, the accepted observations were frozen as the Normal reference corpus. The final corpus contained 516 verified Normal five-minute windows.

The Normal windows were processed using feature schemas corresponding to the incident feature variants so that experimental Stage 1 comparisons used consistent input representations. CAIDA and RPKI/ROV enrichment was subsequently applied to the Normal observations where required, allowing the Normal feature schemas to match the corresponding V1, V2, V3, and V4 incident representations.

Normal observations also retained grouping information designed to prevent overly optimistic evaluation. Where Normal controls were associated with a particular incident context, the grouping strategy conservatively kept the related observations together during TRAIN grouped cross-validation rather than allowing closely related Normal and incident observations to contribute independently across folds.

The resulting Normal corpus provided a controlled reference dataset for evaluating Normal-versus-Incident discrimination, probability calibration, threshold selection, and class/group weighting. However, the subsequent experiments showed that reliable Normal discrimination was not achieved at a level sufficient to justify using Stage 1 as a mandatory gate in the final architecture. The 516-window corpus was therefore preserved as a valid experimental artifact, while the final primary model remained focused on classification and ranking among Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents
CAIDA AS-Relationship Feature Enrichment

The behavioral BGP representation was enriched with historical Autonomous System (AS) relationship information from the Center for Applied Internet Data Analysis (CAIDA). The purpose of this enrichment was to add routing-policy context that is not directly available from raw BGP UPDATE counts or path-length measurements. While behavioral features describe what changed in the routing system, CAIDA relationship information helps characterize whether the observed AS-path propagation is consistent with expected customer-provider and peer-to-peer routing behavior.

Historical CAIDA relationship snapshots were used so that the enrichment reflected the routing-policy context that existed as closely as possible to the time of each incident. This temporal alignment was important because AS relationships and Internet topology change over time. Using only a current relationship dataset to analyze historical incidents could incorrectly assign modern relationships to older AS paths and introduce temporal inconsistency into the feature representation.

For each observed AS path, adjacent AS pairs were mapped to the corresponding inferred CAIDA relationship category where available. These relationships were then aggregated into 14 CAIDA-derived features describing the composition and policy characteristics of the path. The features captured information such as customer-provider and peer-to-peer transitions, relationship-type proportions, policy-transition patterns, and indicators related to whether the observed path was consistent with expected valley-free routing behavior.

Valley-free analysis was included because route leaks often involve propagation that violates normal customer-provider or peer export expectations. However, valley-free violations were not treated as deterministic evidence of a Leak. Real-world routing can contain exceptions caused by complex business relationships, partial transit, route-server behavior, and limitations in relationship inference. Accordingly, valley-free measurements were used as statistical features that contributed contextual evidence to the classifier rather than as hard routing-policy rules.

The enrichment process also preserved unknown or unmapped AS relationships. Adjacent AS pairs that could not be confidently matched to the historical CAIDA relationship data were not forced into an inferred category. Instead, unknown relationships were represented explicitly within the derived features. This prevented missing relationship information from being incorrectly interpreted as a known customer-provider or peer relationship and allowed the model to distinguish between observed policy context and unavailable context.

CAIDA enrichment was applied without modifying the previously frozen behavioral feature values. The resulting feature set formed the V2 representation, consisting of 44 behavioral features plus 14 CAIDA AS-relationship features for a total of 58 features. The enrichment pipeline also supported the later V4 representation, where the same 14 CAIDA features were combined with both the 44 behavioral and 16 RPKI/ROV features.

The contribution of the CAIDA features was evaluated through controlled feature-variant and feature-family ablation experiments rather than assumed in advance. This allowed the study to determine whether AS-policy and valley-free context provided additional discriminatory value for distinguishing among Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents beyond the information contained in behavioral BGP features alone.
RPKI/ROV Feature Enrichment

The behavioral BGP representation was enriched with historical Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) and Route Origin Validation (ROV) information to provide route-origin authorization context for the observed routing behavior. Whereas behavioral features describe changes in BGP activity and CAIDA features provide AS-policy context, RPKI/ROV features characterize whether observed prefix-origin relationships were consistent with the Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) applicable at the time of the routing observation.

The RPKI/ROV enrichment process was designed to preserve historical consistency. Because the incident corpus spans multiple years, current RPKI state could not be applied retrospectively to historical incidents. ROAs can be created, modified, or withdrawn over time, and a prefix-origin pair that is VALID today may have had a different validation state when the incident occurred. Historical RPKI data were therefore aligned with the corresponding BGP observation dates before validation was performed.

The enrichment produced 16 RPKI/ROV-derived features for each five-minute analytical window. These features represented the prevalence and distribution of VALID, INVALID, and NotFound observations and preserved additional information about the reason for INVALID outcomes, particularly origin-AS mismatches and maximum-prefix-length violations. The validation results were treated as contextual model evidence rather than deterministic incident labels.

The RPKI/ROV enrichment was performed without modifying the previously frozen behavioral features. Adding the 16 RPKI/ROV features to the 44 behavioral features produced the V3 feature representation with 60 model features. Combining the same 16 RPKI/ROV features with the 44 behavioral and 14 CAIDA features produced the final V4 representation with 74 model features.
The following subsections describe the historical snapshot mapping, route-origin validation procedure, validation-state representation, and treatment of specific INVALID conditions.
Historical RPKI Snapshot Mapping

Historical RPKI information was aligned with each BGP observation period so that route-origin validation reflected the authorization state that existed at or near the time of the incident. This temporal alignment was necessary because RPKI is not static. ROAs may be published, modified, or withdrawn, and the authorized origin or permitted maximum prefix length may change over time.

For each TRAIN observation date, the enrichment pipeline identified the corresponding historical validated ROA payload information required to evaluate the observed prefix-origin relationships. The complete TRAIN enrichment covered 746 unique observation dates and required 3,730 historical VRP snapshot files. These files were cached locally so that previously acquired historical authorization data could be reused during subsequent enrichment and audit operations.

Historical mapping was performed using the observation date rather than the date on which the experiment was executed. This prevented current RPKI information from being incorrectly applied to historical BGP incidents and reduced the risk of temporal leakage. The same principle was preserved when the enrichment pipeline was later applied to other dataset partitions.

The historical snapshot mapping process was separated from model development. Snapshot selection depended only on the timestamp of the BGP observation and the corresponding historical RPKI data; model predictions, class probabilities, and evaluation results played no role in determining which RPKI information was used.
Route Origin Validation Procedure

Route Origin Validation was performed by comparing each observed BGP prefix, origin AS, and prefix length with the applicable historical RPKI authorization information. The origin AS was derived from the observed AS path, while the advertised prefix and its length were obtained from the corresponding BGP routing observation.

For each prefix-origin observation, the validation procedure first determined whether an applicable historical ROA covered the advertised prefix. If applicable authorization information existed, the observed origin AS and prefix length were compared with the authorized values. This produced one of three principal validation states: VALID, INVALID, or NotFound.

The enrichment pipeline operated on a compact evidence representation created from previously parsed BGP observations. This design avoided repeatedly parsing the complete historical MRT corpus during RPKI enrichment. The full TRAIN enrichment evaluated approximately 79.5 million compact evidence rows representing approximately 129.1 million underlying BGP observations and produced RPKI/ROV features for all 68,031 TRAIN incident windows.

Observation counts were retained in the compact representation so that repeated BGP observations contributed appropriately to the aggregated RPKI features. After validation, observation-level results were aggregated into the corresponding five-minute analytical windows, producing a fixed RPKI/ROV feature schema compatible with the previously frozen behavioral representation.
VALID, INVALID, and NotFound Representation
The route-origin validation procedure assigned observations to three principal RPKI/ROV states: VALID, INVALID, and NotFound.

A VALID observation indicated that an applicable ROA covered the advertised prefix, authorized the observed origin AS, and permitted the advertised prefix length. VALID therefore provided evidence that the observed prefix-origin relationship was consistent with the historical authorization information available for that observation period.

An INVALID observation indicated that an applicable ROA existed but the observed route did not satisfy the authorization. This could occur because the observed origin AS was not authorized or because the advertised prefix was more specific than the maximum prefix length permitted by the applicable ROA.

A NotFound observation indicated that no applicable ROA covered the advertised prefix. NotFound was not interpreted as either legitimate or malicious; it indicated that the available RPKI data provided no applicable route-origin authorization for that observation.

Across the full TRAIN enrichment, the observation-weighted ROV distribution was approximately 64.927% VALID, 0.122% INVALID, and 34.950% NotFound. These distributions illustrate why RPKI states were treated as contextual evidence rather than direct labels. In particular, the relatively small proportion of INVALID observations required the model to combine route-origin evidence with the broader behavioral and AS-policy representation rather than rely solely on RPKI invalidity.

The validation states and their associated counts, ratios, and distributional characteristics contributed to the final set of 16 RPKI/ROV features. These features allowed the model to distinguish among windows containing predominantly authorized observations, uncovered routing observations, and relatively rare authorization conflicts.
Origin-Mismatch and maxLength Evidence

The enrichment process preserved additional information about the reason an observation received an INVALID state. Two principal invalidity conditions were represented: origin mismatch and maximum-prefix-length violation.

An origin mismatch occurred when an applicable ROA covered the observed prefix but the originating AS in the BGP observation was not authorized by the ROA. This condition is particularly relevant to prefix-hijack analysis because an unexpected origin can indicate that address space is being originated by an AS other than the one authorized by the resource holder. However, origin mismatch was not treated as proof of a Hijack because stale ROAs, address transfers, and operational configuration errors can also produce this condition.

A maxLength violation occurred when the observed origin AS was consistent with an applicable authorization but the advertised prefix was more specific than the maximum prefix length permitted by the ROA. This distinction is important because origin authorization and prefix-length authorization represent different dimensions of route-origin validity.

The TRAIN enrichment contained both forms of INVALID evidence, including approximately 112,143 origin-mismatch observations and 44,664 maximum-length-violation observations. Preserving these subtypes allowed the model to distinguish different authorization conflicts rather than representing all INVALID observations as a single undifferentiated category.

The final RPKI/ROV feature schema contained 16 features derived from these validation outcomes and their observation-level distributions. Feature-quality auditing found the representation usable at full TRAIN scale, with 15 features passing the predefined quality criteria and one sparse feature retained for review. The remaining sparse feature was rpki_invalid_maxlength_observation_count, reflecting the relative rarity of maximum-length-invalid observations.

After enrichment, corpus-integrity audits verified that the original behavioral feature values remained unchanged and that the RPKI/ROV features aligned correctly with the corresponding five-minute analytical windows. The resulting V3 and V4 feature representations were then frozen before controlled model development and ablation experiments began.

Each variant was constructed from a frozen feature schema so that model comparisons reflected the addition of specific information sources rather than changes to previously defined features. V1 represented the behavioral baseline and contained only information derived from BGP routing observations. V2 extended this baseline with CAIDA AS-relationship features to evaluate the contribution of routing-policy and valley-free path context. V3 combined the same behavioral baseline with RPKI/ROV features to evaluate the contribution of route-origin authorization evidence. V4 combined all three information sources and represented the complete 74-feature configuration.

The feature schemas were frozen before controlled model comparison. Freezing required the feature names, definitions, ordering, data types, and transformation procedures for each variant to remain unchanged during the corresponding modeling experiments. The original behavioral values were also verified to remain identical when enrichment features were added. This prevented an apparent improvement in an enriched variant from being caused by an unintended modification of the underlying behavioral representation.

Two complementary ablation strategies were used. The first was feature-variant ablation, which compared V1, V2, V3, and V4 under the same model-development conditions. This design allowed the study to evaluate the incremental contribution of the two external enrichment sources. Comparisons between V1 and V2 measured the effect of adding CAIDA information, while comparisons between V1 and V3 measured the effect of adding RPKI/ROV information. V4 then evaluated whether combining behavioral, AS-relationship, and route-origin validation information provided additional value.

The second strategy was feature-family ablation. Rather than comparing only the four broad feature variants, this analysis grouped the V4 features into functionally related families and systematically removed one family at a time while holding the remaining representation constant. The behavioral representation was divided into families representing announcement and UPDATE activity, withdrawal activity, prefix dynamics, peer and visibility behavior, AS-path length and structure, AS-path instability and path change, origin-change and multi-origin behavior, and AS-path prepending. CAIDA AS-relationship and RPKI/ROV information formed two additional feature families.

The feature-family ablation design allowed the study to evaluate whether particular routing-information families contributed uniquely to classification or whether some were redundant with other available evidence. It also provided a more direct measure of feature contribution than relying solely on model-derived importance scores. A reduction in performance after removing a feature family indicated that the removed information contributed useful discriminatory evidence, whereas little change suggested that the information might be redundant with other features.

All feature-variant and feature-family comparisons were performed within the TRAIN development framework using the same incident-level grouped folds and controlled modeling conditions. Validation and Final Holdout data were not used to select feature variants or determine which feature families should be retained. This ensured that feature-selection decisions were based on TRAIN-only evidence and reduced the risk of feature-selection leakage.

The frozen feature-variant design therefore provided a controlled experimental framework for answering one of the central research questions of the Praxis: whether combining behavioral BGP evidence, AS-relationship context, and RPKI/ROV route-origin validation information improves the ability of machine-learning models to distinguish and rank Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents.
Incident Imbalance and Weighting Strategy

Although the final TRAIN corpus was balanced at the incident-class level, with 331 Hijack, 331 Leak, and 331 Outage incidents, the number of five-minute analytical windows associated with individual incidents varied substantially. Some incidents generated considerably more usable BGP observations and therefore contributed more feature rows than others. This created a form of incident representation imbalance that was separate from conventional class imbalance.

Without adjustment, incidents containing large numbers of five-minute windows would contribute proportionally more observations during model training. For example, an incident represented by 200 windows could exert substantially more influence on model fitting than an incident represented by 20 windows, even though both correspond to a single independently labeled routing event. This could cause the model to become disproportionately influenced by longer or more highly observable incidents rather than learning patterns that generalize across the incident population.

Because the BGP incident was defined as the independent experimental unit, the methodology evaluated three controlled imbalance-treatment strategies: I0, I1, and I2. All three strategies used the same TRAIN incidents and grouped cross-validation assignments so that their effects could be compared under consistent experimental conditions.
I0 — Natural Window Representation

I0 preserved the natural distribution of five-minute analytical windows. Every available TRAIN window contributed directly to model fitting without additional incident-level weighting or temporal capping. This strategy retained all available observations and served as the baseline for evaluating the alternative imbalance treatments. However, incidents containing more analytical windows consequently contributed greater aggregate influence during training.
I1 — Incident-Aware Weighting

I1 retained all available analytical windows but adjusted their training weights so that independent incidents contributed approximately equal aggregate influence to the model. For an incident containing analytical windows, the weight assigned to each window was inversely related to the number of windows contributed by that incident. Weights were calculated using only the training portion of each grouped cross-validation fold.

This strategy ensured that a large number of windows from one incident did not cause that incident to have the same influence as multiple independent incidents. Incidents with fewer windows received larger per-window weights, while incidents with many windows received smaller per-window weights. No observations were duplicated, synthetically generated, or removed. I1 therefore preserved the complete temporal information available for each incident while reducing unequal incident influence during model fitting.
I2 — p95 Temporal Cap with Incident-Aware Weighting

I2 combined incident-aware weighting with a temporal cap for incidents containing unusually large numbers of analytical windows. The cap was defined from the TRAIN distribution at the 95th percentile (p95) of incident window counts, corresponding to 164 five-minute windows per incident.

Incidents at or below the p95 threshold retained all available windows. For incidents exceeding the threshold, a temporally distributed subset of windows was retained while preserving coverage across the incident period, including the earliest and latest available observations. Incident-aware weighting was then applied to the retained windows.

The purpose of I2 was to evaluate whether very long incidents contained sufficient redundancy that a controlled temporal cap could reduce their training influence without eliminating the temporal coverage of the incident. The p95 cap was applied only to training folds; observations excluded by the cap were not permanently removed from the underlying corpus, and evaluation folds remained unchanged.
Selection of the Weighting Strategy

The three strategies were evaluated using the same TRAIN incidents, grouped folds, feature configurations, and model-evaluation procedures. Importantly, weighting and temporal capping were applied only during model fitting. Held-out fold observations remained natural, unweighted, and uncapped so that performance was evaluated on the original data distribution.

Both I1 and I2 reduced the disproportionate influence of highly represented incidents. I2 produced the strongest group-level performance in some TRAIN experiments, but its improvement over I1 was relatively small and required excluding a portion of otherwise valid training observations. In contrast, I1 corrected incident-level influence imbalance while retaining the complete set of available five-minute windows.

For this reason, I1 incident-aware weighting was selected for subsequent model development. The strategy provided a balance between controlling unequal incident representation and preserving available routing information. Each independent incident contributed more comparable aggregate influence during training without requiring oversampling, synthetic data generation, or removal of valid observations.

The I0/I1/I2 experiment addressed an important methodological issue in the study: a dataset can be balanced by incident class while remaining imbalanced at the observation level because different incidents generate different numbers of analytical windows. Explicitly controlling this imbalance aligned the model-training process with the incident-level experimental design and reduced the likelihood that a small number of highly represented incidents would disproportionately influence the learned classifier.
Baseline Model Architecture and Model Families

The model-development strategy began with comparatively simple tree-based classifiers and progressively evaluated more specialized architectures. Rather than defining a single model family as the final approach in advance, the methodology treated model architecture as an experimental variable. Random Forest and XGBoost were evaluated because both are well suited to structured tabular data, can model nonlinear relationships among heterogeneous routing features, and can operate effectively without the data volumes typically required by more complex deep-learning architectures.

The model inputs consisted of engineered five-minute feature vectors rather than raw BGP message sequences. Depending on the feature variant, these vectors contained behavioral BGP characteristics, CAIDA AS-relationship information, and RPKI/ROV route-origin validation evidence. This structured representation made tree-based ensemble methods appropriate candidates because they can capture interactions among count, ratio, path, policy, and validation features without requiring extensive feature scaling or transformation.
Single-Stage Random Forest

The first baseline architecture was a single-stage multiclass Random Forest. This model received a feature vector for an analytical window and directly estimated class probabilities for the target incident classes. The single-stage model provided a straightforward baseline against which more complex architectures could be evaluated.

Random Forest constructs an ensemble of decision trees using randomized sampling and feature selection, with the predictions of the individual trees combined to produce the final classification. The approach was selected as an initial baseline because it is robust for structured tabular data, can represent nonlinear feature interactions, and provides a comparatively simple and reproducible reference model (Breiman, 2001).

The purpose of the single-stage Random Forest was not to establish Random Forest as the predetermined final algorithm. Instead, it established a controlled performance reference for determining whether hierarchical classification, alternative imbalance treatments, feature enrichment, hyperparameter optimization, or other model families produced meaningful improvement.
Hierarchical Random Forest Experimental Architecture

A hierarchical Random Forest architecture was also evaluated during the earlier model-development stages. This architecture separated the classification problem into two components. Stage 1 attempted to distinguish Normal from Incident behavior, while Stage 2 classified incident observations as Hijack, Leak, or Outage.

The hierarchical design was motivated by the possibility that separating incident detection from incident-type classification could simplify the learning problem. Stage 1 could theoretically determine whether an observation required incident analysis, while Stage 2 could specialize in distinguishing among the three target incident classes.

This architecture was treated as an experimental candidate rather than the fixed methodology. Subsequent TRAIN-only experiments examined the Stage 1 probability distributions, calibration, decision thresholds, and class/group weighting behavior. These analyses showed that reliable Normal-versus-Incident discrimination could not be established at a level sufficient to justify using Stage 1 as a mandatory gate. Consequently, the hierarchical Random Forest architecture was not retained as the final classification design. The Stage 1 experiments and their methodological treatment are described separately in Section 3.20.
XGBoost

XGBoost was evaluated as a gradient-boosted tree alternative to Random Forest (Chen & Guestrin, 2016). Unlike Random Forest, which builds an ensemble of randomized trees whose predictions are aggregated, XGBoost constructs trees sequentially so that subsequent trees focus on correcting errors made by earlier stages of the ensemble. Regularization, learning-rate control, row subsampling, and feature subsampling provide additional mechanisms for controlling model complexity.

XGBoost was introduced under the same controlled experimental framework used for Random Forest. The same frozen feature representation, incident-aware weighting strategy, grouped folds, incident-level evaluation logic, and ranking metrics were maintained so that differences in performance could be attributed primarily to the learning algorithm rather than changes in the underlying dataset or evaluation procedure.

Both Random Forest and XGBoost were subsequently subjected to bounded hyperparameter optimization and stability analysis using TRAIN data only. The purpose of these experiments was to compare optimized versions of the model families rather than relying solely on default configurations. Final algorithm selection was therefore based on controlled empirical evidence rather than an a priori assumption that one tree-based method was superior.
Rationale for Tree-Based Model Evaluation

Tree-based ensemble models were emphasized because they aligned with several characteristics of the research problem. First, the feature representation was structured and tabular, with the final V4 configuration containing 74 engineered features rather than raw BGP sequences. Second, the independently labeled sample consisted of BGP incidents containing multiple lower-level observations, making data-efficient supervised methods desirable. Third, behavioral, CAIDA, and RPKI/ROV features can interact nonlinearly; for example, an origin change may carry different significance depending on route-origin validity, path behavior, or routing visibility.

Tree ensembles also allowed the study to compare model families while retaining the same feature-engineering and incident-grouping framework. This was important for determining whether performance improvements resulted from the learning algorithm, feature enrichment, weighting strategy, or later incident-level architecture rather than from simultaneous changes to multiple experimental components.

The baseline modeling stage therefore established single-stage Random Forest, hierarchical Random Forest, and XGBoost as controlled candidate approaches. Random Forest provided the initial reference architecture, the hierarchical design tested whether separating Normal-versus-Incident discrimination from incident classification was beneficial, and XGBoost provided a gradient-boosted alternative. Subsequent optimization, stability analysis, and incident-level architecture experiments determined which of these approaches was ultimately carried forward.

Grouped Cross-Validation and Leakage Controls

A central methodological requirement of this study was to ensure that model performance reflected generalization to previously unseen BGP incidents rather than similarity among windows derived from the same incident. Because each incident could generate multiple five-minute analytical windows, conventional random row-level cross-validation was not appropriate. Windows originating from the same incident can share prefixes, peers, origin ASes, AS paths, routing-policy characteristics, and temporal patterns. If these related windows were divided between training and evaluation folds, the model could indirectly observe characteristics of the same incident during both training and testing.

To address this risk, model development used incident-level grouped cross-validation. Each independently labeled BGP incident was assigned a grouping identifier, and all analytical windows associated with that incident remained within the same cross-validation fold. The TRAIN partition was divided into five grouped folds, allowing models to be trained on one set of incidents and evaluated on different incidents. The grouped assignments were frozen and reused across controlled experiments so that changes in performance could be attributed to the experimental condition rather than to different train-test compositions.

The methodology distinguished between the identifier used for model grouping and identifiers used for lower-level analytical observations. Individual five-minute windows retained their own window identifiers for provenance, while the model-group identifier controlled cross-validation membership. This separation allowed many windows from the same incident to contribute information during training without incorrectly treating those windows as independent incidents during evaluation.

The same grouped folds were reused during comparisons of feature variants, imbalance treatments, Random Forest and XGBoost models, hyperparameter configurations, and alternative architectures. Paired comparisons could therefore evaluate two experimental conditions on the same held-out incidents. This reduced variation caused by changing fold composition and provided a more controlled basis for determining whether an observed improvement resulted from the feature set, weighting strategy, or model configuration being tested.
Feature and Weighting Leakage Controls

Feature engineering and imbalance treatment were also constrained by the training boundaries established by grouped cross-validation. Operations that depended on the statistical characteristics of the data were calculated using only the corresponding training portion of each fold where required. For example, incident-aware training weights were constructed from training-fold observations rather than from the held-out fold.

Similarly, the p95 temporal cap evaluated under the I2 imbalance strategy was applied to fold-training observations only. Held-out evaluation data remained natural, unweighted, and uncapped. This ensured that the distribution used for evaluation was not altered to make the classification problem artificially easier.

Feature-variant and feature-family experiments were conducted within TRAIN using the same grouped assignments. Validation and Final Holdout data were not used to determine whether CAIDA, RPKI/ROV, or individual feature families should be retained. This reduced the risk of feature-selection leakage, in which independent evaluation performance influences the feature representation ultimately evaluated.
Hyperparameter and Model-Selection Controls

Hyperparameter optimization was also restricted to the TRAIN development environment. Random Forest and XGBoost searches used the existing grouped folds, frozen V4 feature representation, and I1 incident-aware weighting strategy. Candidate configurations were evaluated without accessing the Final Holdout.

Local refinement experiments were subsequently performed around promising configurations, followed by multi-seed stability analysis of shortlisted candidates. This procedure allowed model configurations to be selected according to repeated TRAIN evidence rather than a single favorable fold or random seed.

The Validation partition was not used as an iterative hyperparameter-tuning dataset. It was accessed under a predefined confirmation protocol after the corresponding TRAIN-developed candidate had been specified. Subsequent architecture development was explicitly versioned as post-Validation TRAIN-only development and did not repeatedly query Validation for model-selection decisions.
Threshold-Selection Leakage Controls

The experimental Normal-versus-Incident Stage 1 introduced an additional potential source of leakage through decision-threshold selection. An earlier threshold value had been selected after observing independent evaluation behavior, which created a threshold-selection concern. The methodology was corrected by requiring candidate thresholds to be derived from TRAIN grouped cross-validation predictions only.

Leakage-safe out-of-fold Stage 1 probabilities were generated for TRAIN, and threshold selection was performed using these predictions rather than Validation or Final Holdout results. The resulting threshold remained an experimental TRAIN-CV proposal and was not treated as part of the final incident-classification architecture. Stage 1 threshold methodology is described further in Section 3.20.
Stacking Leakage Controls

Incident-level stacking introduced a more complex leakage risk because the second-level classifier uses predictions generated by the first-level model. If the first-level model generated training probabilities for observations on which it had already been fitted, the second-level model could learn from unrealistically optimistic first-level predictions.

The stacking methodology therefore used out-of-fold and cross-fit first-level probabilities when constructing incident-level meta-features for model development. First-level predictions used to train the second-level classifier were generated by models that had not been trained on the corresponding held-out incidents. The resulting probabilities were then aggregated into incident-level distributional, confidence, disagreement, and temporal features.

Nested cross-validation was used where required so that second-level training and evaluation maintained the same incident-level separation. Additional forensic audits examined first-level leakage, second-level leakage, uniqueness of incident-level meta-rows, label-derived information, and the possibility of future or post-outcome information entering the meta-feature representation.
Validation and Final Holdout Isolation

The study maintained separate controls for Validation and Final Holdout data. Validation was isolated during the primary model-development process and accessed only under a predefined confirmation protocol. After that evaluation, later architecture development continued using TRAIN data and was explicitly recorded as a separate versioned development phase.

The Final Holdout remained sealed throughout all model-development activities. It was not used for feature selection, imbalance-strategy selection, threshold optimization, algorithm selection, hyperparameter tuning, stacking design, or stability analysis. Before Final Holdout access, the final feature schema, first-level architecture, incident-level meta-feature schema, second-level model configuration, inference procedure, and ranking rule were frozen and subjected to a pre-access audit.

The one-time Final Holdout evaluation was performed only after the pre-access audit passed. No model, feature, weighting, aggregation, ranking, or hyperparameter changes were made after observing the Final Holdout results.

Together, these controls established a leakage-safe experimental hierarchy in which five-minute observations remained grouped by incident, development decisions were made primarily within TRAIN, stacked models used cross-fit predictions, Validation access was controlled, and the Final Holdout remained independent until the complete model was frozen. This methodology was intended to ensure that reported performance represented generalization across BGP incidents rather than memorization of related analytical windows or repeated optimization against independent evaluation data.
Model Optimization and Stability Analysis

Following baseline model comparison, controlled hyperparameter optimization was performed to determine whether the performance of the tree-based classifiers could be improved without changing the frozen feature representation, incident-weighting strategy, or evaluation framework. All optimization was conducted within the TRAIN partition using the same incident-level grouped cross-validation assignments. Validation and Final Holdout data were not used to select hyperparameters.

The optimization process focused on the V4 feature representation with 74 features and the I1 incident-aware weighting strategy, which had been carried forward from the preceding feature and imbalance experiments. Holding these components constant allowed the optimization experiments to isolate the effect of model configuration rather than simultaneously changing the feature space, training distribution, and learning algorithm.
Random Forest Optimization

Random Forest optimization was conducted in two stages. The first stage used a bounded randomized search across 40 predefined hyperparameter configurations. Candidate configurations varied parameters controlling the number of trees, tree depth, feature sampling, minimum leaf size, minimum split size, bootstrap behavior, and split criterion. The existing Random Forest configuration was included as a baseline so that tuned candidates could be compared directly with the previously established model.

Candidate configurations were evaluated using the same five incident-level grouped folds. Selection emphasized incident-level Macro F1, while Top-1 accuracy, Top-2 accuracy, Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR), per-class F1, window-level performance, and computational cost were retained as supporting measures. This prevented model selection from depending exclusively on one aggregate metric.

After the initial search identified a stronger Random Forest configuration, a second local refinement and stability experiment examined a smaller neighborhood around the leading candidate. Rather than performing another broad search, this stage tested a bounded set of nearby configurations and then subjected a shortlist of models to five-seed stability analysis. The objective was to determine whether observed improvements persisted under changes in model randomness rather than resulting from a favorable random seed.

The refined Random Forest candidate used 1,200 trees, maximum depth 40, max_features = 0.30, minimum leaf size 6, minimum split size 6, bootstrap disabled, and the log-loss criterion. This configuration became the strongest Random Forest candidate carried into the subsequent algorithm comparison.
XGBoost Algorithm Comparison and Optimization

XGBoost was then evaluated under the same frozen V4/I1 and grouped-cross-validation framework. The purpose of this experiment was to determine whether gradient boosting provided a meaningful improvement over the refined Random Forest rather than treating XGBoost merely as an untuned baseline.

An initial XGBoost configuration was evaluated, followed by a bounded search across 40 candidate configurations. Parameters included the number of boosting trees, maximum tree depth, learning rate, row subsampling, feature subsampling, minimum child weight, gamma, and L1/L2 regularization. Candidate selection again emphasized incident-level classification and ranking performance while retaining per-class behavior and computational efficiency as secondary considerations.

Following the broad comparison, a separate local XGBoost refinement experiment evaluated 25 configurations around the strongest candidate region. This refinement maintained the same TRAIN incidents, V4 feature schema, I1 weighting, grouped folds, incident aggregation, and evaluation metrics. No Validation or Final Holdout observations were used to guide the refinement.

Multi-Seed Stability Assessment

Multi-seed analysis was used because a single favorable random initialization can produce an overly optimistic estimate of a candidate model's quality. A model was therefore considered more defensible when its performance remained comparatively stable across repeated training runs and across the five grouped folds.

The stability assessment was not used to conduct an unlimited search for the seed producing the highest score. Instead, the same predefined set of seeds was applied to shortlisted candidates, and mean performance and variability were evaluated together. This allowed the study to distinguish reproducible improvements from seed-specific variation.

The refined XGBoost candidate demonstrated stronger TRAIN grouped-CV performance than the refined Random Forest across the principal incident-level classification and ranking measures and was also substantially faster to fit and evaluate. XGBoost was therefore selected as the preferred first-level model family for subsequent incident-level architecture development.
Optimization Stopping Rule

Model optimization was intentionally bounded. Once Random Forest and XGBoost had undergone broad search, local refinement, paired-fold comparison, and multi-seed stability analysis, additional hyperparameter searching was stopped. Continuing to search indefinitely within the same TRAIN folds could progressively overfit the model-development process itself, even without directly accessing Validation or Final Holdout data.

The optimization methodology therefore emphasized controlled improvement and stability rather than maximizing the highest observed cross-validation score. After the refined XGBoost configuration had demonstrated a reproducible advantage over the refined Random Forest, the study shifted from lower-level algorithm tuning to evaluating whether the incident-level architecture could improve how evidence from multiple five-minute windows was combined. That architecture is described in Section 3.18.
Incident-Level Temporal Stacking Architecture

The final architecture combines predictions from multiple five-minute analytical windows into one incident-level classification and ranking. This design was introduced because individual windows provide only partial evidence and simple probability averaging can discard information about confidence, disagreement, and temporal evolution. The final architecture therefore uses two XGBoost levels: a window-level classifier followed by an incident-level classifier.

The architecture can be summarized as: 74-feature V4 window → Level-1 XGBoost → window-level Hijack/Leak/Outage probabilities → incident-level temporal/meta-feature aggregation → Level-2 XGBoost → final class probabilities and ranking. Unlike the earlier experimental hierarchical Random Forest, this architecture does not use Normal-versus-Incident detection as a mandatory first stage.
Level-1 Window Classifier

Level 1 uses the refined XGBoost model with the frozen V4 representation of 74 features: 44 behavioral, 14 CAIDA AS-relationship, and 16 RPKI/ROV features. I1 incident-aware weighting is applied during fitting. For each five-minute window, the model produces probabilities for Hijack, Leak, and Outage. These probabilities are treated as lower-level evidence rather than as the final incident decision.
Cross-Fit Probability Generation

To prevent stacking leakage, TRAIN probabilities used by the second-level model are generated through grouped cross-fitting. Each incident receives first-level probabilities from a model that was not trained on that incident. For final inference, the frozen procedure uses the five TRAIN-fold Level-1 models as an ensemble and arithmetically averages their probabilities before incident-level meta-feature construction.
Incident-Level Meta-Feature Construction

Window-level probabilities are aggregated into one meta-feature row per incident. The frozen schema summarizes probability distributions, prediction confidence, disagreement among windows, and temporal behavior. Ordered windows are divided deterministically into EARLY, MIDDLE, and LATE portions so that changes in class evidence across the incident can be represented. True class labels are not encoded in the meta-features.
Level-2 Incident Classifier

A second XGBoost multiclass classifier receives the incident-level meta-features and produces the final Hijack, Leak, and Outage probabilities. Before Final Holdout access, one deployable Level-2 configuration was selected using a deterministic TRAIN-only rule applied to previously evaluated candidates and was then frozen.
