Classification and Ranking Rule

For each incident, the class with the highest Level-2 probability is reported as the Top-1 classification. The three probabilities are then sorted in descending order to produce the incident ranking. No manually selected decision threshold is required for the final three-class system. This supports evaluation using Macro F1 and class-specific metrics as well as Top-1, Top-2, and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR).

The final architecture therefore separates window-level evidence extraction from incident-level decision-making. Level 1 evaluates the routing evidence within each five-minute window, while Level 2 learns how those predictions combine and evolve across the complete incident.
Nested Stacking and Forensic Leakage Verification

Because the final architecture uses predictions from one model as inputs to a second model, additional controls were required beyond standard grouped cross-validation. The primary risk was stacking leakage, in which Level-2 could receive Level-1 predictions generated by a model that had already been trained on the same incident. This could produce unrealistically strong incident-level performance.

To prevent this, the stacking architecture used nested, incident-grouped cross-validation. Level-1 probabilities used to construct TRAIN meta-features were generated only for incidents excluded from the corresponding Level-1 training fold. These out-of-fold probabilities were then aggregated into incident-level meta-features and supplied to Level-2. Thus, neither analytical windows nor first-level predictions from the evaluated incident were generated using a model trained on that incident.
A separate forensic audit was performed before the architecture was frozen. The audit verified that:
Level-1 probabilities were generated out of fold.
Level-2 training and evaluation preserved incident-level separation.
Each of the 993 TRAIN incidents produced exactly one incident-level meta-feature row.
The TRAIN class distribution remained 331 Hijack, 331 Leak, and 331 Outage.
True class labels were not encoded within the meta-features.
No Validation or Final Holdout information was used to construct or select the stacking architecture.

The architecture was also evaluated across multiple random seeds to determine whether its improvement was stable rather than dependent on a favorable initialization. In addition, a label-permutation test was performed by disrupting the relationship between incident features and class labels. Performance decreased substantially under permutation, providing evidence that the observed classification capability depended on meaningful feature-label relationships rather than leakage or an artifact of the evaluation procedure.

The forensic review also examined the transition between out-of-fold TRAIN probabilities and the probability behavior expected when first-level models were trained for deployment. Any material distributional differences were documented and reviewed before the final inference procedure was frozen. This resulted in the selection of a cross-fit ensemble for Level-1 inference, preserving consistency with the probability-generation strategy used during stacking development.

These procedures provided additional verification that the improvement associated with incident-level stacking resulted from combining legitimate temporal and probabilistic evidence across an incident rather than from information leakage. The final stacking architecture and meta-feature schema were frozen only after these checks were completed successfully.
Experimental Normal-vs-Incident Stage 1

A separate Stage 1 experiment evaluated whether the system could distinguish Normal routing behavior from Incident behavior before performing Hijack, Leak, and Outage classification. Stage 1 was investigated as an auxiliary capability and was evaluated independently from the final three-class incident-ranking architecture. The experiment used the verified Normal corpus described in Section 3.10 and incident observations from the TRAIN partition.
Stage 1 Objective

The objective of Stage 1 was to estimate the probability that an analytical window represented Normal rather than Incident behavior. A Random Forest classifier was evaluated using the frozen feature representation and incident-grouped cross-validation.

The experiment was motivated by the operational possibility of placing an anomaly-screening step before incident classification. However, Stage 1 was required to demonstrate reliable separation between Normal and Incident observations before it could be considered a mandatory component of the final architecture.
Threshold and Calibration Analysis

Because Stage 1 produced probabilities, a decision threshold τ (tau) was required to convert the predicted probability into a Normal-versus-Incident decision. Initial analysis showed that the conventional threshold of τ = 0.50 was poorly aligned with the observed probability distribution.

To avoid threshold-selection leakage, threshold selection was subsequently restricted to TRAIN grouped cross-validation predictions. Calibration and threshold sweeps were performed using leakage-safe out-of-fold probabilities. This procedure produced a TRAIN-CV proposed threshold of τ = 0.06, but fold-specific optimal thresholds varied substantially, ranging from 0.06 to 0.62.

At the proposed threshold, Normal recognition remained weak. The experiment produced Normal precision of approximately 0.036, recall of 0.0078, and F1 of 0.0128. The instability of the threshold and weak Normal performance indicated that threshold adjustment alone did not solve the underlying class-separation problem.
Class-and-Group Weighting

A follow-up TRAIN-only experiment examined whether the problem resulted from unequal effective training influence between Normal and Incident observations. Under the existing group-aware weighting strategy, the effective Incident-to-Normal training-weight ratio averaged approximately 135.24:1.

A class-and-group-balanced condition was therefore evaluated in which Normal and Incident observations received approximately equal total training influence while preserving balanced contribution among independent groups within each class. This adjustment improved Stage 1 ROC-AUC from approximately 0.696 to 0.758, but Normal precision-recall performance remained weak.

The balanced weighting substantially increased the number of observations predicted as Normal without producing sufficiently reliable discrimination. At the resulting TRAIN-CV threshold of τ = 0.72, the false-Normal incident rate remained approximately 26.5%, which was considered operationally unacceptable. The experiment therefore demonstrated that class weighting shifted the predicted probability distribution but did not resolve the underlying Normal-versus-Incident separation problem.
Final Stage 1 Disposition

The Stage 1 experiments showed that neither threshold optimization, probability calibration, nor class-and-group weighting produced sufficiently reliable Normal recognition. The problem was therefore interpreted as a limitation in the discriminatory information available for the Normal-versus-Incident task rather than simply an incorrectly selected value of τ.
Stage 1 was consequently assigned the final status:
UNRESOLVED_EXPERIMENTAL_AUXILIARY

It was not used as a mandatory gate in the final model. The final architecture assumes that a BGP incident has already been identified for analysis and directly classifies and ranks the incident as Hijack, Leak, or Outage. Accordingly, the final incident-level XGBoost stacking architecture does not use a manually selected τ threshold.

The Stage 1 result was retained as an important negative finding because it demonstrates that successful incident-type classification does not necessarily imply reliable general anomaly detection. Developing a streaming or operational Normal-versus-Incident detector remains a separate problem and is identified as an area for future research.

This section describes the controlled transition from model development to independent evaluation. The methodology separated Validation, post-Validation TRAIN-only development, final architecture verification, deployable model freezing, and Final Holdout evaluation so that independent evaluation data did not become part of the iterative model-selection process.
Validation Confirmation Protocol

After TRAIN-only feature selection, model comparison, hyperparameter optimization, and stability analysis, the refined XGBoost candidate was subjected to a single predefined Validation confirmation. Before Validation access, the V4 feature schema, I1 weighting strategy, XGBoost configuration, incident aggregation procedure, evaluation metrics, and minimum acceptance criteria were recorded in a fixed protocol.

The Validation partition contained 213 independent incidents, equally distributed across 71 Hijack, 71 Leak, and 71 Outage incidents. Model fitting remained restricted to the 993 TRAIN incidents. Validation was used only to assess the predefined candidate; it was not used for additional hyperparameter tuning or feature selection.

After the Validation results were observed, no parameters of the evaluated candidate were changed in response to those results. This preserved Validation as an independent confirmation of the model developed during the preceding TRAIN-only experiments.
Post-Validation Versioned Development

Following Validation, the study investigated whether incident-level aggregation could improve upon simple aggregation of window-level predictions. Because this work occurred after Validation had been observed, it was explicitly designated as post-Validation versioned TRAIN-only development.

The incident-level stacking architecture was developed exclusively using the 993 TRAIN incidents with grouped and nested cross-validation. Validation was not reused to select the stacking architecture, meta-features, model family, or hyperparameters, and the Final Holdout remained sealed.

This distinction preserved the experimental chronology. The earlier refined XGBoost model received independent Validation confirmation, whereas the later incident-level stacking architecture was developed and verified using TRAIN-only evidence before its terminal evaluation on the Final Holdout.
Final Architecture Verification

Before the final architecture was frozen, additional TRAIN-only verification was performed to determine whether the improvement from incident-level stacking was reproducible and leakage safe. The verification included nested cross-validation, multi-seed stability analysis, label-permutation testing, first- and second-level leakage audits, and comparison of alternative Random Forest and XGBoost combinations.

Four Level-1/Level-2 combinations were compared: XGBoost→XGBoost, XGBoost→Random Forest, Random Forest→XGBoost, and Random Forest→Random Forest. These comparisons showed that the major improvement was associated with the incident-level stacking architecture, while XGBoost→XGBoost provided the strongest overall classification and ranking performance.
Following these checks, the XGBoost-to-XGBoost architecture was retained as the final architecture candidate. No Validation or Final Holdout data were used during this verification stage.
Deployable Model Freeze

Before Final Holdout access, the study required a fully specified and reproducible deployable model. A pre-access audit initially identified that the incident-level architecture had been frozen but that one unique final Level-2 XGBoost hyperparameter configuration had not yet been specified. Final Holdout access was therefore stopped before any Holdout data were examined.

A short TRAIN-only remediation step recovered the previously evaluated Level-2 candidates and applied a predefined deterministic selection rule. No new hyperparameter search was performed. This process selected the final Level-2 XGBoost configuration and froze the complete model architecture, feature schema, meta-feature schema, cross-fit inference procedure, ranking rule, and hyperparameters.
The completed pre-access audit verified that all required components were frozen before Final Holdout access. Only after the audit passed was the model considered eligible for terminal evaluation.
One-Time Final Holdout

The Final Holdout consisted of 213 previously unseen incidents, equally distributed across 71 Hijack, 71 Leak, and 71 Outage incidents. It remained sealed throughout feature engineering, model selection, hyperparameter optimization, Validation, post-Validation architecture development, stability analysis, and deployable model freezing.

After the pre-access audit passed, the Final Holdout was accessed once using the frozen XGBoost→XGBoost incident-level stacking architecture. TRAIN data were used for model fitting, and the frozen cross-fit ensemble, incident-level meta-feature construction, Level-2 classifier, and ranking procedure were applied without modification.

No feature, weighting, model, hyperparameter, aggregation, or ranking changes were made after the Final Holdout results were observed. The resulting evaluation was therefore treated as the terminal unbiased assessment of the final Praxis model, after which model tuning was considered complete.
Evaluation Metrics

The final model was evaluated using complementary classification and ranking metrics because the system was designed not only to identify the most likely BGP incident type, but also to rank alternative incident classes. Evaluation was performed primarily at the incident level, consistent with the experimental design in which each BGP incident was treated as the independent unit of analysis.

Macro F1 was used as the primary classification metric. Macro F1 calculates the F1 score independently for Hijack, Leak, and Outage and then averages the three values. This gives equal importance to each incident class and prevents overall performance from being dominated by one class.

The ranking capability of the model was evaluated using Top-1 accuracy, Top-2 accuracy, and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR). Top-1 accuracy measures the proportion of incidents for which the highest-ranked predicted class is correct. Top-2 accuracy measures the proportion of incidents for which the correct class appears within the two highest-ranked predictions. MRR evaluates the ranking position of the correct class across all incidents, assigning greater credit when the true class appears closer to the top of the ranked output.

Secondary evaluation measures included class-specific precision, recall, and F1 scores for Hijack, Leak, and Outage. These metrics were used to identify whether performance differed substantially among the three incident classes. Mean true-class rank was also reported as an additional ranking measure, while confusion matrices were used to examine the direction and frequency of classification errors among the three classes.

For the Final Holdout evaluation, a 95% confidence interval was calculated for the primary Macro F1 result to quantify the uncertainty associated with the terminal performance estimate. This provided an additional measure of robustness beyond the single observed score.

ROC, precision-recall, calibration, and threshold-based analyses were used primarily for the experimental Normal-versus-Incident Stage 1 because that problem required evaluation of binary probability separation and decision-threshold behavior. These measures were not the primary evaluation criteria for the final three-class incident-ranking architecture, which used the relative multiclass probabilities directly.

The final evaluation framework therefore emphasized both classification quality and ranking usefulness. Macro F1 measured balanced discrimination among Hijack, Leak, and Outage, while Top-1, Top-2, and MRR measured how effectively the model prioritized the correct incident type within its probability-based ranking.
Computational Latency and Operational Scope

The operational assessment distinguished between the time required to observe and construct BGP features and the computational time required for the final model to classify and rank an incident once those features are available. This distinction is important because the final Praxis uses non-overlapping five-minute analytical windows and therefore should not be interpreted as an instantaneous or full real-time anomaly-detection system.

The final architecture is best characterized as a POST-WINDOW INCIDENT CLASSIFICATION system. BGP UPDATE observations must first be collected, assigned to the appropriate five-minute analytical windows, and transformed into the required Behavioral, CAIDA, and RPKI/ROV feature representation. Once the necessary first-level probabilities and incident-level information are available, the downstream K1 stacking computation is comparatively fast.

A dedicated latency experiment measured the warm downstream K1 computational path from available first-level probability information through incident-level meta-feature construction and final ranking. The measured mean processing time was approximately 25.6 milliseconds per incident, with a median of approximately 24.8 milliseconds and a 95th-percentile latency of approximately 27.6 milliseconds. This corresponds to an approximate downstream processing capacity of about 39 incidents per second under the tested environment.

The latency measurement should not be interpreted as the complete end-to-end detection time. It excluded raw BGP UPDATE collection, MRT parsing, five-minute observation-window accumulation, initial feature extraction, model loading, and other live data-ingestion overhead. Operational latency is therefore expected to be dominated primarily by the time required to accumulate the necessary routing evidence and construct the feature representation rather than by the final incident-ranking computation itself.

The latency experiment was performed in a macOS environment using Python 3.12.2 and XGBoost 3.4.1, with 11 processing threads reported by the test environment. The benchmark used cached TRAIN-derived probability and meta-feature artifacts to isolate the computational cost of the downstream classification and ranking stages.

Accordingly, the present system should be interpreted as demonstrating that incident classification is computationally inexpensive once the required five-minute BGP evidence has been constructed, rather than demonstrating complete real-time BGP detection within milliseconds. Future work may extend the architecture toward streaming UPDATE ingestion, incremental feature computation, and earlier partial-window classification to evaluate end-to-end time-to-detection and time-to-stable classification in operational environments.
Methodological Limitations
Several methodological limitations should be considered when interpreting the results of this study.

First, the research relies on historical public BGP observations and documented incident labels. RouteViews provides broad Internet routing visibility, but its collectors do not observe every route from every network. Collector placement, participating peers, and routing policies therefore influence the BGP evidence available for each incident. Similarly, documented Hijack, Leak, and Outage labels represent the best available incident classification but do not provide direct access to every affected router or the complete operational context of each event.

Second, the external enrichment sources also contain inherent limitations. CAIDA AS relationships are inferred from observable Internet routing behavior and may not represent every private or complex interconnection agreement. RPKI/ROV information provides evidence about route-origin authorization, but historical RPKI coverage is incomplete, and an INVALID state does not necessarily indicate malicious activity. These sources were therefore treated as contextual features rather than definitive incident labels.

Third, the final model is limited to the three incident classes evaluated in the study: Hijack, Leak, and Outage. Other BGP conditions, including configuration errors, traffic-engineering changes, session instability, and additional forms of routing anomalies, were not modeled as independent final classes. The system should therefore not be interpreted as a universal classifier for all possible BGP problems.

Fourth, reliable Normal-versus-Incident detection remained unresolved. Although a verified Normal corpus was constructed and threshold, calibration, and weighting strategies were evaluated, Stage 1 did not achieve sufficient discrimination to serve as a mandatory gate. The final architecture therefore assumes that a candidate BGP incident has already been identified and focuses on classifying and ranking its incident type.

Finally, the methodology uses five-minute analytical windows and evaluates the final system as a post-window incident classifier. The measured model-side processing latency demonstrates that classification and ranking are computationally fast once the required information is available, but the study did not evaluate complete end-to-end latency from live BGP UPDATE arrival through streaming feature generation and final prediction. Real-time detection and sub-five-minute classification therefore remain areas for future research.

These limitations define the intended interpretation of the methodology: the proposed system is an AI-assisted BGP incident classification and ranking framework based on observable control-plane evidence, rather than a complete real-time detection, physical root-cause determination, or automated mitigation system.
Chapter Summary

This chapter described the methodology used to develop and evaluate the AI-based BGP incident classification and ranking system. The research followed an incident-centered experimental design in which Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents served as the independent experimental units, while non-overlapping five-minute windows provided the lower-level observations used for feature engineering and model development.

Historical BGP UPDATE data were obtained from RouteViews and processed through controlled acquisition, parsing, quality-gate, and five-minute windowing procedures. The resulting behavioral representation contained 44 BGP features and was enriched with 14 historical CAIDA AS-relationship features and 16 historical RPKI/ROV features, producing the final 74-feature V4 representation. Controlled feature variants and ablation experiments were designed to measure the contribution of each source of routing evidence.

The methodology also addressed differences in the number of analytical windows contributed by individual incidents. Three imbalance strategies were evaluated, with I1 incident-aware weighting retained because it reduced unequal incident influence while preserving all available training observations. Random Forest and XGBoost models were then compared, optimized, and evaluated for stability using TRAIN-only incident-grouped cross-validation.

The final architecture uses incident-level temporal stacking. A Level-1 XGBoost model generates Hijack, Leak, and Outage probabilities for individual five-minute windows. Cross-fit probabilities are subsequently transformed into incident-level features representing probability distributions, confidence, disagreement, and temporal behavior. A Level-2 XGBoost classifier uses this representation to produce the final incident classification and probability-based ranking.

Particular attention was given to preventing data leakage. The methodology incorporated incident-level grouping, nested cross-validation, out-of-fold probability generation, multi-seed stability analysis, forensic stacking audits, independent Validation, model freezing, and a sealed Final Holdout. A separate Normal-versus-Incident Stage 1 experiment was also conducted, but its discrimination performance was insufficient for inclusion as a mandatory component of the final architecture.

Finally, the methodology distinguished model computation time from operational observation time. The final system is characterized as a post-window incident classification and ranking framework: five-minute BGP observations and their associated features must first become available, after which the downstream incident-level classification and ranking computation requires approximately 25.6 milliseconds per incident in the measured environment.

Together, these procedures established a reproducible and leakage-controlled methodology for evaluating whether behavioral BGP information, AS-policy context, route-origin validation evidence, and incident-level temporal aggregation can support accurate classification and ranking of BGP incidents. Chapter 4 presents the experimental results produced by this methodology.

The ablation results therefore show that no single feature family completely determined incident classification. Behavioral BGP features provide the underlying control-plane observations, while CAIDA and RPKI/ROV features contribute additional policy and security context. The results also demonstrate that the value of these information sources depends on both the evaluation metric and the incident class being considered.

These findings directly address RQ2/H2 by demonstrating that specific BGP and contextual feature families provide measurable discriminatory information for distinguishing Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents, with RPKI/ROV showing the strongest overall ablation contribution in this TRAIN-only experiment.
Incident Imbalance and Weighting Results

Although the TRAIN corpus was balanced at the incident-class level, individual incidents contributed different numbers of five-minute analytical windows. Without adjustment, incidents containing more windows could exert greater influence during model fitting than incidents represented by fewer windows. Three TRAIN-only strategies—I0, I1, and I2—were therefore evaluated to determine how incident representation should be handled.

I0 retained the natural window distribution without incident-level weighting or temporal capping. This preserved all observations but allowed incidents with large numbers of windows to contribute proportionally more training weight.

I1 retained all available windows while applying incident-aware weighting. Window weights were adjusted inversely to the number of windows contributed by each incident so that incidents had more comparable aggregate influence during model fitting. This approach preserved the complete temporal evidence while reducing the dominance of highly represented incidents.

I2 combined incident-aware weighting with a p95 temporal cap of 164 windows per incident. Incidents exceeding the threshold were represented by a temporally distributed subset of their windows before weighting was applied. This strategy tested whether reducing potentially redundant observations from unusually long incidents could further improve incident-level generalization.
Table 4.5 Incident Imbalance Strategies Evaluated

The comparison showed that controlling incident representation was preferable to allowing the natural window distribution to determine training influence. Both I1 and I2 reduced the disproportionate contribution of incidents containing large numbers of analytical windows.

I2 produced slightly stronger group-level results in some TRAIN comparisons, indicating that limiting unusually long incidents could reduce redundant training information. However, the improvement over I1 was not sufficiently large or consistent to justify permanently discarding otherwise valid analytical windows. I2 also introduced an additional temporal-sampling decision into the training pipeline.

In contrast, I1 preserved every available five-minute window while directly addressing the underlying imbalance problem. It therefore provided a simpler and more conservative approach: all available routing evidence remained available to the classifier, while each independent incident contributed more comparable aggregate influence during model fitting.

For these reasons, I1 was selected as the final incident-imbalance strategy and was combined with the V4 feature representation for subsequent Random Forest and XGBoost development. The resulting V4/I1 configuration established the controlled development baseline used for model optimization and algorithm comparison.

Importantly, weighting was applied only during model fitting. Held-out grouped-CV observations remained natural and unweighted, ensuring that the evaluation distribution was not altered to favor the selected strategy. Experimental Stage 1: Normal-vs-Incident Results

The experimental Stage 1 analysis evaluated whether verified Normal routing windows could be reliably distinguished from windows associated with Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents. Stage 1 was evaluated separately from the final three-class classification architecture. The results showed that although weighting and threshold adjustments improved some discrimination measures, Normal-versus-Incident separation remained insufficient for use as a mandatory first-stage gate.
Initial Stage 1 Performance

The initial Stage 1 classifier was evaluated using leakage-safe TRAIN grouped cross-validation. The analysis revealed substantial overlap between the predicted probability distributions for Normal and Incident observations. As a result, the conventional probability threshold of 0.50 did not provide reliable Normal recognition.

This limitation was particularly evident in the precision-recall behavior of the Normal class. Although the classifier contained some discriminatory information, the probability distributions were not sufficiently separated to produce both acceptable Normal recognition and a low rate of incidents incorrectly classified as Normal.

The results motivated two additional experiments: a controlled TRAIN-only threshold analysis and a class-and-group weighting experiment designed to determine whether the observed limitation resulted primarily from the decision threshold or from unequal effective training influence between Normal and Incident observations.
τ Threshold Analysis

The Stage 1 decision threshold, τ (tau), determines the probability boundary used to convert model output into a Normal-versus-Incident classification. To prevent threshold-selection leakage, τ was selected using out-of-fold predictions generated exclusively from TRAIN grouped cross-validation.

The TRAIN-CV analysis proposed τ = 0.06. However, the optimal thresholds differed substantially across the five grouped folds: 0.06, 0.62, 0.32, 0.32, and 0.45. This variation demonstrated that the threshold was not stable across independent groups of TRAIN incidents.
At the proposed τ = 0.06 threshold, Normal-class performance remained weak. Normal precision was approximately 0.0360, recall was approximately 0.0078, and F1 was approximately 0.0128.
Table 4.6 Stage 1 TRAIN-CV Threshold Results

The combination of low Normal F1 and substantial fold-to-fold threshold variation indicated that the problem could not be resolved simply by selecting a different value of τ. The analysis therefore shifted to whether the training-weight structure itself was limiting Stage 1 discrimination.

Class-and-Group Weighting

A follow-up weighting experiment evaluated whether the poor Normal performance resulted partly from unequal effective training influence between Normal and Incident observations. The revised condition, designated W1, balanced class-level influence while preserving group-aware weighting.

The weighting adjustment improved ROC-AUC from approximately 0.6963 to 0.7581, indicating better overall separation between Normal and Incident probability distributions. However, PR-AUC increased only from approximately 0.0140 to 0.0162, demonstrating that performance on the difficult Normal class remained weak.

Under W1, the TRAIN-CV threshold shifted to τ = 0.72. Despite the improvement in ROC-AUC, approximately 26.52% of incident observations were incorrectly classified as Normal under the resulting decision rule. For an operational screening stage, this represented an unacceptable failure mode because a mandatory Stage 1 gate could prevent a substantial number of actual incidents from reaching the downstream Hijack/Leak/Outage classifier.

The W1 results therefore demonstrated an important distinction between improved ranking separation and operationally useful binary classification. The increase in ROC-AUC showed that weighting improved the model's ability to order Normal and Incident observations, but the very low PR-AUC and high false-Normal rate showed that the probability distributions remained insufficiently separated for reliable gating.

UNRESOLVED_EXPERIMENTAL_AUXILIARY

Stage 1 was not incorporated as a mandatory gate in the final architecture. Instead, the final system assumes that a candidate BGP incident has already been identified and directly classifies and ranks it as Hijack, Leak, or Outage. Consequently, the final XGBoost incident-level stacking architecture does not use τ = 0.06, τ = 0.72, or any other manually selected Normal-versus-Incident threshold.

This negative result is methodologically important. It demonstrates that strong classification among known BGP incident types does not necessarily imply that the same feature representation can reliably distinguish arbitrary Normal routing behavior from incident behavior. Stage 1 therefore remains a separate anomaly-detection problem and is identified as an area for future research.

Incident-Level Stacking Results

Following independent Validation, the study examined whether the predictions generated across multiple five-minute windows could be combined more effectively at the incident level. The refined window-level XGBoost model provided useful classification evidence, but simple aggregation could discard information about probability distributions, prediction confidence, disagreement among windows, and changes in class evidence over time.

Phase K1 therefore compared a simple mean-probability aggregation baseline (K1-B0) with an incident-level temporal stacking architecture. This work was explicitly conducted as post-Validation, TRAIN-only development. Validation was not reused for architecture selection, and the Final Holdout remained sealed.
Mean-Probability Baseline

The K1-B0 baseline represented each incident by taking the arithmetic mean of its window-level class probabilities. The resulting average probabilities were then used to classify and rank Hijack, Leak, and Outage.
K1-B0 achieved an incident-level Macro F1 of 0.802937, Top-1 accuracy of 0.804632, Top-2 accuracy of 0.935549, and MRR of 0.891574. Hijack F1 was 0.750853.

The baseline demonstrated that aggregating window probabilities could produce a useful incident-level decision. However, averaging reduced each incident to a small number of mean values and did not explicitly represent the distribution, confidence, disagreement, or temporal evolution of predictions across the incident.
Temporal Stacker

The K1 temporal stacker retained additional information from the window-level probability sequence. Cross-fit Level-1 probabilities were transformed into incident-level meta-features representing probability distributions, confidence, disagreement, and deterministic EARLY, MIDDLE, and LATE temporal behavior. A second XGBoost classifier then generated the final incident-level probabilities.
The selected temporal stacking candidate achieved an incident-level Macro F1 of 0.934666, Top-1 accuracy of 0.934542, Top-2 accuracy of 0.992951, and MRR of 0.966096.

The improvement was observed across both classification and ranking measures. Top-2 accuracy increased to approximately 99.3%, indicating that the correct incident class was almost always contained within the two highest-ranked predictions during the TRAIN-only nested evaluation.

No Level-2 leakage was detected during incident-level model development. Grouped and nested evaluation preserved incident separation, and the meta-feature dataset contained exactly 993 unique incident-level rows, corresponding to the 993 TRAIN incidents.

The concentration of errors between Hijack and Leak is also consistent with the routing characteristics represented in the feature space. The distinction therefore depends on the combination of behavioral evidence with route-origin authorization and AS-policy context rather than on a single routing indicator. The feature-ablation results in Section 4.3 similarly showed that RPKI/ROV information had its strongest measured class-specific contribution to Hijack discrimination.

Outage produced substantially fewer classification errors. Only two of the 71 Outage incidents were assigned an incorrect Top-1 classification, and both were classified as Hijack. One Final Holdout incident, Hijack:68538, received a processing status of REVIEW because no directly relevant RouteViews observations were identified during one processing check. The error analysis reinforces the distinction between Top-1 classification and ranked diagnostic support. Although 17 incidents were incorrect at Top-1, the true class was ranked second for 15 incidents and third for only two. Consequently, the correct class remained within the first two ranked alternatives for 211 of 213 Final Holdout incidents. The remaining errors therefore affected the ordering of competing hypotheses more frequently than they completely excluded the correct incident type from the model's highest-ranked alternatives.

Overall, the Final Holdout errors were concentrated in a relatively interpretable pattern, with Hijack-versus-Leak discrimination representing the principal residual challenge. This finding provides a specific direction for future feature development while preserving the strong overall Final Holdout classification and ranking performance.
Computational Latency and Operational Feasibility

The computational assessment evaluated how quickly the final K1 architecture could produce an incident classification and ranking after the required model inputs were available. This distinction is important because computational inference latency is different from the total time required to collect BGP UPDATE messages, construct five-minute analytical windows, generate features, and identify a candidate incident.

Phase N measured the warm downstream K1 computational path from available Level-1 probability information through incident-level meta-feature construction and final ranking. The mean processing time was approximately 25.58 milliseconds per incident, with a median of approximately 24.77 milliseconds and a 95th-percentile latency of approximately 27.63 milliseconds.

Accordingly, the final architecture is characterized in this Praxis as post-window incident classification. The system operates after the required BGP observation windows and model inputs have become available. Its measured computational latency demonstrates that the downstream classification and ranking stage can execute quickly, but it does not establish end-to-end real-time anomaly-detection latency.

This distinction is also relevant to the five-minute analytical window used throughout the study. The five-minute interval defines the temporal resolution at which the final feature representation was trained and evaluated; it does not imply that the model requires five minutes of computation. Once the required information is available, the measured downstream processing requires only tens of milliseconds.

A production implementation could potentially reduce operational latency by processing BGP UPDATE messages continuously and maintaining Behavioral, CAIDA, and RPKI/ROV features incrementally as observations arrive. However, sub-five-minute or streaming classification was not evaluated in the present study and therefore remains an area for future research.

Overall, the Phase N results demonstrate that the final K1 architecture has low post-feature computational overhead. Operational deployment latency would be dominated primarily by BGP observation, feature construction, and data-pipeline processing rather than by the final incident-level classification and ranking computation.
Mapping Results to Research Questions

The experimental results can be mapped directly to the research questions and hypotheses established in Chapter 1. This mapping distinguishes between conclusions supported by the completed experiments and broader operational claims that were not directly measured.
RQ1/H1 — BGP Incident Classification and Ranking

RQ1 examined whether machine-learning models could classify and rank likely BGP incident types using observable routing evidence. H1 proposed that machine learning could accurately rank and explain the likely incident classes.

The terminal Final Holdout provides the primary evidence for this question. Across 213 previously unseen incidents, the frozen XGB→XGB architecture achieved a Macro F1 of 0.920177, Top-1 accuracy of 0.920188, Top-2 accuracy of 0.990610, and MRR of 0.958529.

The correct class was ranked first for 196 incidents and within the first two positions for 211 of 213 incidents. These results support the classification and ranking component of RQ1/H1 and demonstrate that the model generalized to incidents that were not used during model development.
RQ2/H2 — Contribution of Routing Feature Families

RQ2 examined which BGP and contextual features contributed to distinguishing among incident types. H2 proposed that specific routing features would provide discriminatory information for Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents.

The V1–V4 feature experiments and feature-family ablation provide evidence for this question. The RPKI/ROV-enriched V3 achieved the highest feature-variant Macro F1 of 0.545986, while the complete V4 representation achieved the strongest Top-2 and MRR among the four feature variants.

Feature-family ablation provided additional evidence. Removing RPKI/ROV produced the largest overall Macro-F1 decrease of 0.022411 and reduced Hijack F1 by 0.031304. Peer-visibility behavior produced the largest measured effect on Leak F1, while CAIDA AS-relationship features produced the largest measured effect on Outage F1.

These results support RQ2/H2 by showing that different routing-information families contributed measurable and class-dependent discriminatory information. The findings indicate predictive contribution rather than causal proof of incident type.
RQ3/H3 — Value of Incident-Level Aggregation
RQ3/H3 examined whether the proposed incident-level ranking approach improved diagnostic classification compared with a simpler representation of the available BGP evidence.

The K1 experiment provides the strongest direct evidence for this question. The mean-probability aggregation baseline achieved a TRAIN nested-CV Macro F1 of 0.802937. Incorporating probability distributions, confidence, disagreement, and temporal information through the incident-level stacker increased Macro F1 to 0.934666, an improvement of 0.131729.

Top-1 increased from 0.804632 to 0.934542, Top-2 increased from 0.935549 to 0.992951, and MRR increased from 0.891574 to 0.966096. The temporal stacker also outperformed the mean-probability baseline in all five grouped folds.

These results support the predictive-performance component of RQ3/H3 by demonstrating that incident-level aggregation provided substantially stronger classification and ranking than simple probability averaging. However, the study did not conduct a controlled experiment measuring human troubleshooting time or MTTR against log- or SNMP-based workflows. Therefore, any claim that the system reduces operational diagnostic time should be presented as a potential operational benefit rather than as an experimentally demonstrated outcome.

This chapter presented the experimental results from the development, verification, and final evaluation of the proposed BGP incident classification and ranking system. The experiments progressed from feature and imbalance analysis through Random Forest and XGBoost optimization, independent Validation, incident-level temporal stacking, forensic verification, architecture comparison, and terminal Final Holdout evaluation.

Feature experiments showed that behavioral BGP, CAIDA AS-relationship, and RPKI/ROV information provided complementary evidence. V3 achieved the highest feature-variant Macro F1, while V4 produced the strongest ranking performance. Feature-family ablation further showed that removing RPKI/ROV produced the largest overall Macro-F1 decrease and the largest measured reduction in Hijack F1. Incident-aware weighting (I1) was subsequently retained because it controlled unequal incident representation while preserving all available five-minute windows.

Model optimization established XGBoost as the preferred window-level classifier. Independent Validation revealed a meaningful generalization decrease, particularly for Hijack, but satisfied the predefined confirmation criteria. Rather than concealing this decrease, the result motivated post-Validation TRAIN-only investigation of how evidence from multiple five-minute windows was combined.

Incident-level temporal stacking produced the largest architectural improvement in the study. Macro F1 increased from 0.802937 with mean-probability aggregation to 0.934666 with temporal stacking, while Top-2 increased to 0.992951. Multi-seed analysis, nested cross-validation, label-permutation testing, and forensic leakage audits supported the stability and validity of this improvement. Comparison of four RF/XGBoost stacking combinations subsequently identified XGB→XGB as the strongest overall architecture.

The frozen model was then evaluated once on the sealed 213-incident Final Holdout. It achieved a Macro F1 of 0.920177, with a 95% confidence interval of [0.880117, 0.954402], Top-1 accuracy of 0.920188, Top-2 accuracy of 0.990610, and MRR of 0.958529. The correct incident class appeared within the first two ranked predictions for 211 of 213 incidents. Final errors were concentrated primarily between Hijack and Leak, with Hijack remaining the most difficult class.

Finally, Phase N showed that once the required routing evidence and model inputs were available, the downstream K1 classification and ranking computation required approximately 25.58 milliseconds per incident on average. This result represents post-feature computational latency rather than end-to-end live detection latency. The completed system is therefore characterized as a post-window incident classification and ranking architecture.

Overall, the results demonstrate that heterogeneous routing evidence and incident-level temporal aggregation can support accurate and stable classification and ranking of Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents.
