Chapter 5 — Conclusions
Overview

This Praxis investigated whether machine learning can assist enterprise network operations by classifying and ranking the most likely type of a BGP routing incident using evidence derived from BGP UPDATE messages. The research was motivated by the difficulty of interpreting BGP control-plane behavior when different incidents can produce overlapping symptoms, such as changes in AS paths, routing instability, withdrawals, origin changes, and changes in prefix visibility.

The study developed an incident-centered machine-learning framework that combines three complementary sources of routing information: behavioral BGP features, CAIDA AS-relationship and routing-policy context, and RPKI/ROV route-origin validation evidence. These features were evaluated using independently labeled Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents, with incident-level partitioning and leakage controls used throughout model development and evaluation.

A major finding of the study was that the representation of an incident across time was important. Rather than treating each five-minute analytical window as an independent final decision, the completed architecture uses window-level XGBoost probabilities as evidence for an incident-level temporal stacking model. The final system produces probabilities for Hijack, Leak, and Outage and orders those probabilities to provide a ranked set of incident hypotheses for further investigation by a network engineer.

The scope of the completed system is important to define clearly. The final architecture is not a general-purpose real-time BGP anomaly detector and does not independently determine whether arbitrary routing behavior is Normal or anomalous. The experimental Normal-versus-Incident Stage 1 did not demonstrate sufficient discrimination to be retained as a mandatory component of the final architecture. Instead, the final system assumes that a candidate BGP incident has already been identified and then classifies and ranks that incident as Hijack, Leak, or Outage.

Similarly, the system should not be interpreted as proving the physical root cause of a network failure. Its predictions are based on observable BGP control-plane evidence and external routing context. The ranked output is intended to serve as an AI-assisted diagnostic layer that helps prioritize the incident explanations an operator should investigate, while router logs, configuration state, telemetry, security information, and engineering judgment remain necessary for complete operational diagnosis.

The final architecture is therefore characterized as a post-window incident classification and ranking system. Once the required five-minute routing evidence and model inputs are available, classification and ranking are computationally fast. Extending the framework toward streaming anomaly detection, earlier classification, and integration with live enterprise telemetry represents a natural direction for future research.

This chapter interprets the findings in relation to the research questions, identifies the principal contributions of the Praxis, discusses their practical implications for network operations, examines the limitations and threats to validity, and presents future research and operational extensions.
Mapping of Findings to Research Questions and Hypotheses

The findings of this Praxis provide evidence that BGP incident diagnosis benefits from combining multiple forms of routing information and evaluating that evidence at the incident level rather than treating individual routing observations as independent final decisions. Chapter 4 presented the quantitative results for each experiment. This section interprets those findings in relation to the research questions and hypotheses and defines the conclusions that can reasonably be drawn from the study.
RQ1/H1 — BGP Incident Classification and Ranking

RQ1 asked how machine-learning models can classify, rank, and explain likely BGP incident types using observable routing evidence. H1 proposed that machine learning could accurately rank and explain the likely incident classes.

The Final Holdout results provide the strongest evidence for this question. The frozen model achieved a Macro F1 of approximately 0.9202, Top-2 accuracy of 0.9906, and MRR of 0.9585 across 213 previously unseen incidents. More operationally meaningful than any single aggregate metric is the ranking result: the correct incident class appeared among the model's first two ranked alternatives for 211 of 213 incidents.

This finding supports the use of probability-based ranking rather than relying exclusively on a single predicted label. In network operations, several BGP incidents can produce overlapping control-plane symptoms. A ranked output allows the system to communicate both its preferred interpretation and a secondary alternative. For example, when Hijack and Leak evidence overlap, presenting both hypotheses in probability order can provide more useful investigative guidance than returning only one categorical prediction.

The results therefore support RQ1/H1 for classification and ranking. However, the term root cause should be interpreted within the scope of the available BGP evidence. The model identifies the most likely incident class—Hijack, Leak, or Outage—rather than proving the underlying physical or administrative cause. Complete diagnosis may still require router logs, configuration state, topology information, telemetry, and operator investigation.
RQ2/H2 — Contribution of Routing Evidence

RQ2 examined which BGP and contextual features contribute to distinguishing among routing incidents. H2 proposed that specific routing features would provide useful discriminatory evidence for Hijack, Leak, and Outage.

The results show that feature contribution was more nuanced than simply adding more features and observing a corresponding increase in every performance metric. The behavioral-only V1 representation established the baseline. Adding RPKI/ROV information in V3 produced the highest feature-variant Macro F1, while the complete V4 representation containing Behavioral, CAIDA, and RPKI/ROV features produced the highest Top-2 accuracy and MRR among the feature variants.

This distinction is important. V4 did not achieve the highest Macro F1 simply because it contained the largest number of features. Instead, different information sources influenced classification and ranking in different ways. Behavioral features described what changed in BGP, CAIDA features added AS-relationship and routing-policy context, and RPKI/ROV features provided information about whether observed prefix-origin relationships were consistent with historical authorization.

Feature-family ablation strengthened this interpretation. Removing RPKI/ROV produced the largest overall decrease in Macro F1, and its removal also produced the largest measured decrease in Hijack F1. This is consistent with the role of route-origin authorization in distinguishing unexpected or unauthorized origin behavior. At the same time, other feature families contributed differently across Leak and Outage incidents, demonstrating that no single routing indicator was sufficient for all three classes.

The results therefore support RQ2/H2 as a predictive feature-contribution finding. They do not establish that RPKI invalidity, a valley-free violation, or any other individual feature proves a particular incident type. Instead, the model benefits from combining multiple forms of evidence whose importance varies according to the routing behavior being analyzed.
RQ3/H3 — Value of Incident-Level Temporal Aggregation
RQ3/H3 examined whether combining evidence across an incident could improve classification and ranking compared with a simpler aggregation of window-level predictions.

This produced one of the strongest findings of the Praxis. The mean-probability baseline achieved a TRAIN nested-CV Macro F1 of approximately 0.8029. When the same underlying window-level predictions were represented using incident-level probability distributions, confidence, disagreement, and temporal information, Macro F1 increased to approximately 0.9347. The improvement occurred in all five grouped folds and was subsequently supported by multi-seed stability and forensic leakage testing.

The significance of this result extends beyond the numerical improvement. A BGP incident is not naturally represented by a single five-minute observation. Routing evidence can develop over time as announcements, withdrawals, paths, origins, and visibility change. Simple probability averaging compresses this behavior into a mean and discards information about whether predictions are stable, conflicting, concentrated, or changing across the incident. Temporal stacking preserves more of this structure and allows the model to evaluate the incident as a sequence of related observations.

The architecture-comparison experiment further showed that the improvement was not solely an XGBoost effect. Random Forest/XGBoost combinations using the same stacking concept also performed strongly, although XGB→XGB provided the best overall balance. This supports the interpretation that incident-level representation itself was a major source of improvement.

These findings support the predictive-performance component of RQ3/H3. However, the original hypothesis also proposed that the system would reduce diagnostic time and improve accuracy relative to traditional log- or SNMP-based troubleshooting. The present study did not conduct a controlled experiment involving network engineers or directly measure troubleshooting time, MTTR, or human diagnostic accuracy. That portion of H3 therefore cannot be claimed as experimentally demonstrated.

Instead, the current results establish the prerequisite technical finding: incident-level temporal aggregation substantially improves automated classification and ranking of BGP incidents. Whether this improvement translates into faster human diagnosis or reduced MTTR should be evaluated through a future controlled operator study comparing conventional troubleshooting with AI-assisted ranked incident analysis.

Overall, the three research questions converge on a common conclusion. The effectiveness of the proposed approach depends not on a single algorithm or feature, but on the combination of heterogeneous routing evidence and incident-level representation. Behavioral BGP information provides the observable routing activity, CAIDA and RPKI/ROV add policy and security context, and temporal stacking combines evidence distributed across multiple analytical windows into an operator-oriented incident ranking.
Summary of Key Contributions

This Praxis makes several methodological and operational contributions to the application of machine learning for BGP incident analysis. The primary contribution is not a new BGP protocol or security mechanism, but an integrated framework for transforming public BGP control-plane observations and external routing context into an incident-level, probability-based diagnostic ranking.
Incident-Centered BGP Machine-Learning Methodology

The first contribution is an incident-centered experimental methodology for BGP machine learning. Rather than treating millions of five-minute routing observations as independent experimental samples, the study treats the documented BGP incident as the primary unit of analysis.

All windows associated with an incident remain together during dataset partitioning and grouped cross-validation. TRAIN, Validation, and Final Holdout are also separated at the incident level. This design reduces the risk that highly related observations from the same routing event appear in both model development and evaluation and produce overly optimistic performance estimates.
The methodology therefore provides a framework for evaluating whether a model generalizes to previously unseen routing incidents, rather than merely to unseen rows from previously observed incidents.
Integration of Behavioral, CAIDA, and RPKI/ROV Evidence
The second contribution is the integration of three complementary forms of routing evidence into a common machine-learning representation.

The final V4 feature schema combines 44 behavioral BGP features, 14 historical CAIDA AS-relationship features, and 16 historical RPKI/ROV features, producing a 74-feature representation. Behavioral features describe observable routing activity; CAIDA features provide AS-relationship and routing-policy context; and RPKI/ROV features provide historical route-origin authorization evidence.

An important aspect of this contribution is temporal alignment. Historical CAIDA and RPKI information was mapped to the corresponding incident periods rather than applying present-day routing context retrospectively to historical events.

The feature experiments further demonstrated that these sources provide different forms of predictive information. In particular, RPKI/ROV produced the strongest overall feature-family ablation effect and the largest measured contribution to Hijack discrimination.
Incident-Aware Weighting Methodology

The third contribution is the explicit treatment of incident representation imbalance. Even when the number of incidents per class is balanced, individual incidents can generate substantially different numbers of five-minute windows. Without correction, incidents containing many windows can exert greater influence during model training than incidents represented by fewer observations.

The I1 incident-aware weighting strategy addressed this problem by adjusting window-level training influence according to the number of observations contributed by each incident. This allowed all valid analytical windows to remain in the training data while making the aggregate influence of independent incidents more comparable.

This distinction between class imbalance and incident representation imbalance is particularly relevant to machine-learning studies based on high-volume network telemetry, where one underlying event may generate thousands or millions of correlated observations.
Leakage-Safe Incident-Level Temporal Stacking
The fourth contribution is the development of a leakage-safe incident-level temporal stacking architecture.

Rather than using individual five-minute classifications as the final output or simply averaging their probabilities, the architecture summarizes window-level predictions using probability distributions, confidence, disagreement, and deterministic EARLY, MIDDLE, and LATE temporal characteristics. A second-level classifier then uses this representation to produce the final incident decision.

The architecture was developed using cross-fit probabilities and nested incident-level evaluation to prevent Level-1 predictions from leaking training information into Level 2. Multi-seed analysis, label-permutation testing, and forensic leakage audits were subsequently used to verify the observed improvement.
The substantial improvement over mean-probability aggregation demonstrates that how evidence is combined across an incident can be as important as the individual window-level classifier itself.
Probability-Based Incident Ranking for Network Operations

The fifth contribution is an operationally oriented probability-based ranking output. Instead of returning only a categorical label, the final system produces probabilities for Hijack, Leak, and Outage and ranks the three incident hypotheses.

This design reflects the uncertainty inherent in BGP diagnosis. Different incident types can produce overlapping control-plane behavior, and the available public routing evidence may not always support a single unambiguous conclusion. A ranked output allows an operator to see both the model's preferred explanation and the most plausible alternatives.

The Final Holdout result, in which the correct class appeared within the first two ranked alternatives for 211 of 213 previously unseen incidents, demonstrates the practical value of evaluating the system as a ranking framework rather than solely as a conventional classifier.
Experimental Corpus and Reproducibility Framework

A supporting contribution is the construction and management of a balanced experimental corpus containing 1,419 independently labeled incidents, with 473 Hijack, 473 Leak, and 473 Outage incidents. The corpus was partitioned into 993 TRAIN, 213 Validation, and 213 Final Holdout incidents and processed through a documented quality-control and provenance framework.

The study also produced frozen feature schemas, experiment registers, decision records, evidence maps, leakage audits, reproducibility checks, and authoritative result artifacts. Together, these materials provide traceability from incident construction through final evaluation.

The corpus itself should not be characterized as a publicly available research dataset unless it is formally released with sufficient provenance and documentation. The contribution demonstrated by the present Praxis is therefore more appropriately described as the corpus-construction and reproducibility framework, together with the resulting experimental foundation used to evaluate the proposed methodology.

Taken together, these contributions extend beyond the performance of a particular classifier. The Praxis demonstrates an end-to-end methodology for organizing BGP incidents as independent experimental units, enriching behavioral observations with historically aligned routing context, controlling unequal incident representation, combining temporal evidence without leakage, and translating model probabilities into ranked diagnostic hypotheses that can support network-engineering investigation.
Practical Implications for Network Operations

The practical value of the proposed system is its ability to transform BGP control-plane observations into a prioritized set of incident hypotheses that can support a network engineer's investigation. Traditional monitoring systems are effective at identifying routing changes and generating alerts, but an alert alone may not explain what type of routing incident most likely produced the observed behavior. The proposed model is intended to operate as an additional diagnostic layer within this workflow.
BGP telemetry → monitoring/alert → candidate incident → feature generation → AI classification and ranking → ranked Hijack/Leak/Outage hypotheses → engineer investigation

In this architecture, existing monitoring systems would continue to identify routing events or conditions requiring investigation. Once sufficient routing evidence was available, the model would analyze the behavioral, AS-relationship, and route-origin validation features and produce probabilities for the three incident classes.

For example, a model output might rank the incident as Hijack = 0.71, Leak = 0.24, and Outage = 0.05. This output provides more operational information than a generic message such as “BGP anomaly detected.” The engineer can begin by investigating evidence consistent with a Hijack while recognizing that Leak remains a plausible secondary explanation. The ranking therefore functions as an investigative prioritization mechanism rather than an automated declaration of physical root cause.

The feature representation can also provide useful context for the investigation. A high Hijack probability can be examined alongside origin changes and RPKI/ROV evidence, while a Leak hypothesis can be evaluated against AS-relationship, propagation, and valley-free characteristics. An Outage prediction can direct attention toward withdrawal, visibility, and routing-instability behavior. This creates a connection between the model's ranked output and routing information that is meaningful to network operations.

The model is intended to complement rather than replace existing operational telemetry. Router logs remain important for identifying BGP session transitions and device-level events. Border Gateway Protocol Monitoring Protocol (BMP) feeds can provide detailed routing telemetry, while SNMP and streaming telemetry provide information about interface, device, and protocol state. SIEM platforms can correlate routing behavior with security events, and configuration-management systems can identify policy or configuration changes occurring near the incident period. These sources provide information that cannot be inferred reliably from public BGP UPDATE observations alone.

An enterprise implementation could therefore combine the model's output with router logs, BMP, SNMP or streaming telemetry, SIEM events, configuration state, topology information, and operator knowledge. The AI-generated ranking would help determine which evidence should be examined first rather than replacing these sources or automatically performing remediation.

The computational results also support this type of integration. Phase N measured approximately 25.6 milliseconds per incident for the warm downstream K1 computation after the required first-level probability information was available. This indicates that the final classification and ranking computation itself is lightweight enough to support operational workflows.

However, the 25.6-millisecond measurement is not end-to-end detection latency. It does not include BGP UPDATE collection, five-minute observation-window accumulation, feature generation, CAIDA or RPKI/ROV enrichment, or other live data-pipeline processing. The final architecture should therefore be characterized as computationally fast after the required routing information is available, not as a system that detects BGP incidents in approximately 25 milliseconds.

The current implementation is consequently best viewed as a post-window decision-support system. In a future production architecture, BGP telemetry could be processed continuously and features maintained incrementally, allowing the ranking model to be invoked as soon as sufficient evidence becomes available. Such an implementation could integrate with existing network-management or observability platforms and present the ranked hypotheses as part of an incident alert, dashboard, or troubleshooting workflow.

From an operational perspective, the principal contribution is therefore not autonomous troubleshooting. It is the ability to convert complex routing evidence into a small, probability-ranked set of incident hypotheses that gives the network engineer a more focused starting point for investigation. Whether this capability measurably reduces troubleshooting time or MTTR compared with existing operational workflows remains an important question for future controlled evaluation
Limitations of the Study

Although the results demonstrate strong classification and ranking performance, several limitations define the boundaries within which the findings should be interpreted. These limitations relate primarily to public BGP visibility and incident ground truth, uncertainty in external routing-context datasets, the restricted set of incident classes, and the post-window operational scope of the final architecture.
Public Collector Visibility and Incident Ground Truth

The study relies primarily on historical BGP UPDATE observations obtained from RouteViews. Public route collectors provide broad visibility into Internet routing behavior but do not observe every route from every Autonomous System or network location. Collector placement, participating peers, routing policies, and route propagation therefore influence the evidence available for individual incidents.

Incident labels also depend on documented historical information rather than direct access to every affected router, configuration, or network operator. Hijack, Leak, and Outage labels represent the best available classification of the documented incidents, but public BGP telemetry alone cannot establish every physical, administrative, or configuration-level cause.

One Final Holdout incident, Hijack:68538, received a REVIEW status during a processing check because directly relevant RouteViews observations were not identified in that specific check. The incident nevertheless produced valid V4 feature rows and remained evaluable within the frozen pipeline, while the final schema and reproducibility audits passed. This case is retained as a documented data-quality caveat rather than treated as evidence that the aggregate Final Holdout result was materially affected.
Historical CAIDA and RPKI/ROV Uncertainty

The external enrichment datasets also introduce uncertainty. CAIDA AS-relationship information is inferred from observable Internet routing behavior and therefore cannot represent every private, complex, or changing commercial relationship between Autonomous Systems. A relationship classified as customer-provider or peer-to-peer should consequently be interpreted as inferred routing-policy context rather than an authoritative description of a private interconnection agreement.

RPKI/ROV information has similar limitations. Historical RPKI coverage is incomplete, and an RPKI INVALID state does not by itself demonstrate malicious routing behavior. Operational configuration errors, ROA maintenance, prefix-length inconsistencies, and other legitimate conditions can also result in invalid states.

The methodology reduced temporal inconsistency by aligning CAIDA and RPKI/ROV information with historical incident periods as closely as practical. Nevertheless, these features remain contextual evidence rather than definitive ground-truth indicators.
Restricted Incident-Class Scope

The final model classifies and ranks three incident classes: Hijack, Leak, and Outage. These classes represent important BGP routing incidents but do not encompass the complete range of conditions encountered in enterprise and Internet routing operations.

BGP session resets, configuration errors, route-policy changes, planned maintenance, prefix deaggregation, traffic-engineering changes, upstream connectivity failures, and other routing disturbances can generate control-plane behavior that overlaps with the three modeled classes.

The final model should therefore not be interpreted as a universal BGP root-cause classifier. Its probability output ranks the three incident hypotheses represented in the experimental corpus. Applying the model to conditions outside this scope could cause an unmodeled event to be assigned to the most similar learned class. Expanding the incident taxonomy is therefore an important direction for future research.
Post-Window and Offline Operational Scope

The completed architecture uses five-minute analytical windows derived from historical BGP observations. The system was evaluated primarily through offline experiments rather than through continuous production deployment against a live enterprise BGP telemetry stream.

The approximately 25.6-millisecond mean downstream K1 latency measures computation after the required routing information and first-level probability evidence are available. It does not include live BGP UPDATE collection, accumulation of the five-minute analytical window, behavioral feature generation, CAIDA and RPKI/ROV enrichment, model initialization, or other production data-pipeline delays.

The final system is therefore characterized as POST-WINDOW INCIDENT CLASSIFICATION, not as an end-to-end real-time detection system. The latency results demonstrate that the downstream classification and ranking computation is relatively inexpensive once the necessary evidence has been prepared, but they do not establish complete operational time-to-detection or time-to-diagnosis.

The use of five-minute windows also establishes the temporal resolution evaluated in this Praxis. The study did not determine whether equivalent classification performance could be achieved using shorter observation intervals or partial incident evidence. Determining how early a stable and correct incident classification can be produced remains an important area for future research.

These limitations define the boundaries within which the findings of this Praxis should be interpreted. The study demonstrates that observable BGP behavior, combined with historically aligned AS-policy and route-origin validation evidence, can support accurate classification and ranking of Hijack, Leak, and Outage incidents under the evaluated conditions. The findings do not establish universal BGP anomaly detection, physical root-cause determination, or end-to-end real-time operational performance. Extending the framework to broader incident classes, streaming telemetry, additional enterprise data sources, and live operational evaluation remains an important direction for future research.
Recommendations for Future Research

The results of this Praxis establish a foundation for BGP incident classification and ranking, but several extensions are necessary to move the framework from historical post-window analysis toward broader operational use. Future work should focus on reducing the time required to produce a reliable classification, expanding the types of incidents and telemetry available to the model, and evaluating whether ranked predictions improve the troubleshooting performance of network engineers.
Streaming and Incremental Feature Processing

The current methodology constructs features from completed five-minute analytical windows. A natural next step is to convert the pipeline into a streaming feature-processing architecture in which BGP UPDATE messages are processed continuously as they arrive.
BGP UPDATE stream → incremental feature updates → contextual CAIDA/RPKI enrichment → continuously updated model probabilities → incident-level ranking

Instead of reconstructing features after an observation window has completed, announcement counts, withdrawal rates, AS-path statistics, origin changes, prefix visibility, and related behavioral features could be maintained incrementally. CAIDA relationship information and validated RPKI/ROV data could be maintained as locally cached contextual datasets and joined with incoming routing observations as required.

This architecture could allow the model to update its Hijack, Leak, and Outage probabilities continuously as new evidence becomes available. The objective would not necessarily be to eliminate the five-minute representation immediately, but to determine whether equivalent or sufficiently reliable predictions can be generated before the complete analytical window has elapsed.
Early Incident Classification and Time-to-Stable Prediction

A particularly important future experiment is to determine how much routing evidence is required before the model can produce a stable and correct incident classification. The present study establishes performance using five-minute analytical windows and incident-level temporal aggregation but does not determine the earliest point at which sufficient evidence becomes available.
30 seconds → 1 minute → 2 minutes → 3 minutes → 5 minutes → full incident-level K1 horizon

At each interval, the system could be evaluated using the same primary metrics used in this Praxis: Macro F1, Top-1 accuracy, Top-2 accuracy, and MRR. Performance could then be plotted as a function of elapsed observation time.

A particularly useful new operational metric would be Time-to-Stable-Correct-Classification (TSCC). TSCC could measure the earliest point at which the correct incident class reaches the required ranking position and remains stable as additional routing evidence becomes available. For example, an incident might initially be ranked as Leak, transition to Hijack after 90 seconds, and remain Hijack for the rest of the observation period. TSCC would capture this behavior more meaningfully than reporting only the final five-minute classification.

This experiment would help determine whether the current five-minute observation interval can be shortened and would provide a more direct measure of the tradeoff between diagnostic speed and classification reliability.
Real-Time Normal-versus-Incident Detection

The experimental Stage 1 analysis showed that Normal-versus-Incident classification remains a separate challenge. Rather than forcing the current incident classifier to perform this task, future research should investigate a purpose-built streaming anomaly-detection layer.

Potential approaches include online change-point detection, streaming anomaly-detection algorithms, adaptive baselines, unsupervised or semi-supervised learning, and models specifically trained on a broader and more representative corpus of Normal routing behavior.
Continuous BGP monitoring → anomaly/change detection → candidate incident → Hijack/Leak/Outage ranking

This separation would allow the anomaly detector to specialize in identifying meaningful deviations from normal routing behavior while the classification architecture developed in this Praxis focuses on determining which incident hypothesis best explains the detected event.
Broader Incident Classes and Enterprise Telemetry

The current model is restricted to Hijack, Leak, and Outage. Future research should expand the incident taxonomy to better represent the range of problems encountered by enterprise network engineers. Candidate classes could include BGP session resets, routing-policy or configuration errors, prefix deaggregation, traffic-engineering changes, and upstream connectivity failures.

Expanding the incident classes should also be accompanied by integration of additional enterprise telemetry. Public BGP UPDATE data provide valuable control-plane evidence but cannot reveal every device-level or physical condition associated with an incident.

Future models could combine BGP observations with BMP feeds, router logs, SNMP or streaming telemetry, interface state, configuration changes, topology information, and SIEM events. These sources could provide evidence about BGP session state, interface failures, policy changes, device health, and security events that are not directly observable through public route collectors.
Such multimodal operational evidence could move the framework beyond ranking routing-event classes and closer to physical and configuration-level root-cause diagnosis.
Explainability and Operator Evaluation

Future work should also expand the explainability component of the system. Feature-attribution methods such as SHAP could be used to present the routing evidence contributing most strongly to an incident prediction. An operator could then see not only that Hijack is ranked first, but also whether the prediction is associated with origin changes, RPKI/ROV evidence, AS-path instability, visibility changes, or other relevant routing characteristics.

More importantly, the operational value of the system should ultimately be evaluated with network engineers performing realistic troubleshooting tasks. A controlled study could compare traditional troubleshooting with a workflow augmented by AI-assisted ranked incident diagnosis.

Evaluation measures could include time to correct diagnosis, diagnostic accuracy, number of investigative steps, operator confidence, and frequency of incorrect investigative paths. The experiment could also evaluate whether explanations improve operator trust and whether engineers appropriately challenge incorrect model recommendations rather than accepting them automatically.

Such an evaluation would directly test the operational portion of the original H3 that could not be demonstrated in the present study. The current Praxis establishes that the model can accurately classify and rank incidents; a future operator study could determine whether those predictions actually help engineers diagnose incidents faster and more accurately in realistic network operations.

Together, these extensions provide a progression from the current post-window classification framework toward a more complete operational system: streaming telemetry, earlier classification, independent anomaly detection, broader incident coverage, richer enterprise evidence, explainable predictions, and direct evaluation with network engineers.
Conclusion

BGP telemetry provides network operators with detailed evidence of what changed in the routing system, but determining which type of incident most likely explains those changes remains difficult. Hijacks, route leaks, and outages can produce overlapping patterns of announcements, withdrawals, AS-path changes, origin changes, and routing instability. This Praxis investigated whether machine learning could combine these signals into a practical incident classification and ranking framework.

The completed approach integrates behavioral BGP features, CAIDA AS-relationship and routing-policy context, and RPKI/ROV route-origin validation evidence within a common analytical representation. BGP observations were organized into five-minute windows, classified using XGBoost, and subsequently combined through incident-level temporal stacking. This architecture allowed evidence distributed across multiple routing observations to be transformed into ranked probabilities for Hijack, Leak, and Outage.

The terminal evaluation demonstrated that the approach generalized to previously unseen incidents. On the sealed 213-incident Final Holdout, the frozen architecture achieved a Macro F1 of 0.9202, Top-2 accuracy of 0.9906, and MRR of 0.9585. The correct incident class appeared among the first two ranked alternatives for 211 of 213 incidents, demonstrating the value of presenting probable incident types as a prioritized ranking rather than relying only on a single categorical prediction.

The results also demonstrate that the effectiveness of the system depends on more than the choice of machine-learning algorithm. Historically aligned routing-security and AS-policy information contributed additional discriminatory evidence, while incident-aware weighting reduced unequal influence among incidents. Most importantly, incident-level temporal stacking substantially improved performance over simple averaging of window-level probabilities, demonstrating the value of analyzing the evolution and consistency of routing evidence across an incident.

The Praxis does not solve universal BGP anomaly detection, nor does it claim to determine the physical root cause of every routing event. The final system assumes that a candidate incident has been identified and uses the available control-plane evidence to rank the most likely incident type. Router logs, configuration state, network telemetry, security information, and engineering judgment remain necessary components of complete operational diagnosis.

The principal conclusion of this Praxis is therefore that machine learning can provide an effective post-window diagnostic ranking layer for BGP incident analysis. By converting behavioral, policy, and route-origin validation evidence into a prioritized set of incident hypotheses, the proposed approach provides network engineers with a more focused starting point for investigation and establishes a foundation for future streaming, explainable, and enterprise-integrated BGP diagnostic systems.
